This thesis addresses the challenge of conducting molecular property prediction when the underlying experimental data, or ``labels'' are noisy.
Most work on noise in QSAR modeling assumes Gaussian label noise and evaluates either representations or model architectures in isolation.
[CIT] examined 12 algorithms across multiple noise levels but used fixed representations, and studies that compare representations typically use clean data.

No work has systematically compared the relative importance of representation versus architecture choice for label noise robustness, asked whether probabilistic methods justify their computational overhead under noise, or tested whether findings generalize across different types of injected noise.
This thesis fills that gap.
I will also discuss noise mitigation, using the results of my noise robustness study.
I explore why many noise mitigation techniques underperform in cheminformatics data and methods to address this problem in the form of novel molecular representations.
The first half of this thesis therefore asks four questions.

First, how does the choice of molecular representation and model architecture explain the variance in predictive performance, and does that division change when you instead consider how much performance a QSAR model is able to retain under increasing label noise?
Second, what does the choice of model provide with label noise?
Within this question we compare the effects of deterministic and probabilistic modeling.
Third, does the type of label noise matter, or just the quantity of it?
We explore different techniques of generating and adding label noise to both clean data, as well as data with inherent experimental noise.
Fourth, what is the impact of artificial label noise on a model's uncertainty estimation?
Does the estimated uncertainty rise with increased label noise and can these uncertainty values point to which labels are corrupted?
Together, these questions aim to identify what, if anything, makes a QSAR model robust to noise.
To answer them we introduce NoiseInject, an open-source Python package for benchmarking noise robustness and uncertainty quantification (Section [REF]).

How can the best set of features be selected for a given dataset and model, and does the method carry over from small molecules to antibodies and reactions?

This chapter describes the molecular representations and models we use, molecular similarity and activity cliffs, the sources of label noise, how we inject noise, the methods for learning with noisy labels, the NoiseInject package and how results are evaluated.
The success of machine learning hinges on the quality of input data.
Although the quality can refer to noise, which the majority of our work is centered around, in this case we are talking about the type of input.
Molecular representations provide different features with which QSAR models and noise detection techniques can be learned.
However, a potential bottleneck on larger datasets should be noted; the more complex the data structure, the greater the computational cost.
For smaller datasets, the number of parameters is limited by the size of the training set, to prevent overfitting.

text: Alternative representations that capture different structural, chemical, or physical features are able to overcome these limitations.
Recent advances have led to the development of new molecular fingerprints.
One such method is the Sort \& Slice (SNS) technique, an alternative to hash-based folding for pooling ECFP substructures [CIT].
Sort \& Slice begins by sorting all circular substructures in the training set according to their frequency of occurrence.
It then ``slices'' away all but the N most frequent substructures, which are subsequently used to generate an N-dimensional, bit-collision-free binary fingerprint.
This approach solves the ambiguity problem of hashed fingerprints, where multiple substructures might be encoded at the same bit position, making it very interpretable [CIT].
Sort \& Slice fingerprints outperform ECFP of diameter four (ECFP4) with standard hash-based folding methods across various molecular property prediction tasks.
These experiments consisted of different data splitting techniques, machine learning models, fingerprint diameters, fingerprint dimensions, and atomic invariants [CIT].
Furthermore, Sort \& Slice outperformed advanced substructure selection schemes such as filtered fingerprints and mutual information maximization [CIT].
Neural fingerprints are a category of learned representations that overcome the fixed, hard-coded nature of traditional fingerprints.
Unlike ECFP or MACCS keys, which rely on predefined hashing schemes or substructure catalogs, neural fingerprints train on molecular data to capture chemical information [CIT].
These representations are the result of deep learning architectures that have learned dense, continuous embeddings which can be used for downstream tasks.
Mol2vec, which adapts the Word2vec algorithm from NLP to molecular substructures [CIT], is a common neural fingerprint.
Mol2vec treats molecules like ``sentences'' and circular substructures derived from Morgan fingerprints like ``words''.
The model learns vector embeddings for each substructure through unsupervised training, such that chemically similar substructures are mapped to nearby points in the embedding space [CIT].
The embeddings of all present substructures are summed to obtain a full representation.
This approach produces 300-dimensional dense vectors that avoid the sparsity and bit collisions inherent in hashed fingerprints [CIT].
Mol2vec has performed strongly on various QSAR benchmarks, matching or exceeding Morgan fingerprints on solubility and bioactivity prediction tasks [CIT].

Neural fingerprints provide several advantages over traditional fingerprints.
They produce dense continuous vectors that avoid sparseness and information loss from bit collisions [CIT].
They can also be pre-trained once on large unlabeled datasets and then fine-tuned for specific downstream tasks, opening the door to transfer learning [CIT].
However, pre-training them is computationally expensive, and they are less directly interpretable than fingerprints, although attention visualization offers some insight [CIT].
Beyond fingerprints, physicochemical-descriptor vectors (PDVs) are a class of continuous-value molecular descriptors that encode structural and chemical properties of molecules [CIT].

Unlike binary fingerprints or graph-based representations, PDVs aggregate atom and bond-level quantities into fixed-length feature vectors that capture a wide variety of information about a molecule and its structure [CIT].

PDVs typically consist of hundreds of properties including constitutional descriptors such as molecular weight, atom and bond counts, and heteroatom ratios; topological indices encoding molecular connectivity patterns; physicochemical properties such as logP (lipophilicity), molar refractivity, and topological polar surface area; and electronic descriptors derived from partial charges and polarizabilities [CIT].
The RDKit cheminformatics toolkit provides a comprehensive suite of more than 200 molecular descriptors that cover these categories [CIT].
Many PDV descriptors, such as logP, molecular weight and partial charges, have a direct physicochemical meaning, although many of the thousands available have no clear interpretation [CIT].

They are also less computationally expensive than some 3D methods or neural fingerprints, with many descriptors simply requiring a 2D molecular structure without conformer generation or extensive pre-training.
This efficiency makes PDVs particularly appropriate for high-throughput applications.
Descriptors based on 3D structure can also be used [CIT].
However, PDVs have limitations.
The dimensionality of PDV feature spaces can lead to problems with multicollinearity [CIT].
This can be mitigated by feature selection or dimensionality reduction techniques [CIT].

Additionally, PDVs encode molecular properties as aggregated global features, which may not capture fine-grained structural details such as specific substructure arrangements or local chemical environments, information important for particular endpoints.
One of the more intuitive representations is the molecular graph.
These graphs can be categorized into 2D and 3D graphs.

2D graphs rely on adjacency matrices that encode topological atom- and bond-level features but leave out geometric properties such as bond angles or torsion, meaning they may fail to capture stereochemistry.
3D graphs incorporate these spatial features, but are often limited by remaining in a single conformation [CIT].
A standard molecular graph is constructed such that each molecule is represented as G = (V,E) with node features x_i and edge features e_ij.
In one common featurization, nodes encode atom type, chirality, hybridization and aromaticity, and edges encode bond type, ring membership, direction and stereochemistry [CIT].

text: Voxel-based 3D representations, in which each atom occupies one grid cell, are too sparse for convolutional networks to perform well; [CIT] instead spread each atom over nearby voxels with a wave transform.
These graph representations do not highlight specific substructures or specific arrangements of atoms and bonds within each molecule.
The substructures contain functional groups that are related to a range of chemical properties and are potentially involved in downstream tasks related to the function of molecules.
[CIT] developed graph substructure networks, a topologically aware message passing scheme based on substructure encoding.
The method involves encoding structural roles based on the appearance of specific substructures and using them in message passing updates.
Since message-passing graph neural networks (GNNs) are at most as powerful as the Weisfeiler--Lehman test, they cannot isolate sufficient features from the graph structure [CIT].
Graph substructure networks, on the other hand, capture these substructure-related features.
Encoders pretrained on unlabeled molecules, whether graph-based [CIT] or transformers on SMILES [CIT], can also produce embeddings that capture structural features.
There are a wide variety of model architectures that can be used for QSAR modeling.
Starting off with simpler and more explainable models, we have tree-based methods.
Decision trees are non-parametric supervised learning algorithms that perform recursive binary partitioning of the feature space [CIT].

A decision tree builds a predictive model by learning a series of if-then rules that recursively split the data based on given feature values, creating a tree where internal nodes represent decision rules, branches represent the results of those decisions, and leaf nodes contain predicted values or class labels [CIT].
Each recursive split is chosen to maximize homogeneity within the resulting partitions.
For classification, Gini impurity is commonly used and for regression, mean squared error reduction [CIT].
There are several properties that make decision trees a good foundation for QSAR modeling.
First, they handle non-linear relationships between molecular descriptors and target properties without requiring explicit feature engineering or transformation [CIT].

They also do not make assumptions about the underlying distribution of the data, making them robust to violations of parametric assumptions that can limit linear regression or other classical methods [CIT].
Decision trees handle data in a ``contributory'' rather than ``consensus'' manner.
In consensus methods such as linear regression or neural networks, every data point influences the prediction at every other point in the feature space.
Tree-based methods make predictions based on the subset of training samples that fall into the same leaf node as the test point [CIT].
This mechanism essentially quarantines outliers in their respective leaf nodes, limiting their impact on predictions for samples in other regions or chemical domains.
Individual decision trees tend to have high variance and often overfit, particularly at large depths [CIT].
Small modifications made to the training data can result in large differences in the structure of the tree, resulting in unstable predictions [CIT].
Ensemble methods are used to counteract this instability, aggregating predictions from many trees.
Random forests (RFs) aggregate predictions from trees trained on bootstrap samples of data with random subsets of features at each split [CIT].
Bootstrapping ensures that each tree is trained on a slightly different subset of data, which effectively reduces the influence of any individual sample [CIT].
This is especially beneficial with noisy samples.
The selection of random features at every node decorrelates the trees, which lowers the generalization error of the ensemble [CIT].
The aggregation of trees further prevents overfitting to noise by smoothing out prediction errors from individual noisy labels.
Neural networks (NNs), a very popular family of models, can also be used for QSAR, although with mixed results.
An NN is a system of interconnected nodes which learn by passing information through its layers.
There are weights and biases attached to the nodes and various other parameters which the model optimizes to minimize the difference between the predicted output and the actual target value.
During training, the network parameters are updated using backpropagation, in which gradients of the loss function with respect to each weight are propagated backward through the network [CIT].
The structure of these networks and the hyperparameters used depend on the type of NN.

In QSAR, one of the most commonly used architectures is the multilayer perceptron (MLP), an NN containing fully-connected layers with non-linear activation functions which transforms molecular feature vectors (i.e., fingerprints, descriptors) into a property or activity prediction [CIT].

text: Various approaches have been proposed to improve neural network robustness to label noise, including noise-robust loss functions [CIT], confident learning to identify mislabeled examples [CIT], and regularization techniques such as mixup [CIT] or label smoothing [CIT].
All the models up to this point have assumed a vector-based input.
Molecular graphs, on the other hand, require different types of predictive modeling.
Two standard ML methods on molecular graphs include Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs).
GCNs apply the concept of convolution to graph-structured data.
Instead of operating on grid-based data, such as images, GCNs aggregate information from neighbors of a node to update its representation [CIT].
In contrast, GINs address the limitations in GCNs’ ability to differentiate between non-isomorphic graphs.

Unlike GCNs, which normalize and weight the sum of neighboring node features, GINs use a simple sum followed by a trainable MLP, giving the model flexibility to learn complex transformations of node features.

The GIN model’s design is informed by the Weisfeiler--Lehman test for graph isomorphism, enabling it to distinguish between molecular graphs that are structurally similar but differ in subtle ways [CIT].

GIN features have been competitive with or better than fingerprints and descriptors at classifying pairs of molecules as activity cliffs (ACs; Section [REF]), where small variations in molecular structure can lead to significant changes in chemical or biological activity [CIT].
Descriptor-based models still predicted the potency of cliff molecules better than deep learning methods [CIT].
Gradient boosting methods such as eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) sequentially fit trees to the residuals of previous iterations, progressively reducing the prediction error [CIT].
We used a handful of gradient-boosted tree ensembles in this thesis including Light Gradient-Boosting Machine (LightGBM) [CIT], and Natural Gradient Boosting (NGBoost) [CIT].
Support vector regression fits a function that is as flat as possible while keeping training errors small [CIT].
It uses the -insensitive loss, under which errors smaller than cost nothing and larger errors cost their size minus .
A constant C trades flatness against tolerance of large errors [CIT].
The features enter the model only through the kernel.
With the radial basis function (RBF) kernel, every feature enters the Euclidean distance between two molecules.
In Chapter [REF] the continuous representations are standardized and the binary fingerprints are used as built.
Three properties limit the effect of a wrong label: errors inside the tube change nothing, the loss outside it grows linearly, and the weight of each molecule is capped at C [CIT].
Under simulated experimental error, the RBF-kernel SVM degraded smoothly and linearly [CIT].
Its main limitation is computational cost, because training operates on a kernel matrix that grows with the square of the number of training molecules [CIT].

Standard feed-forward networks are deterministic; however, they can be transformed into probabilistic models (Figure [REF]).
Unlike standard deterministic ML methods, Bayesian methods model distributions over predictions using Bayes' rule, allowing for the quantification of uncertainty within parameters and labels.
Bayesian methods treat the model parameters as random variables with distributions.
Uncertainty can also be estimated from other non-deterministic methods, including deep ensembles [CIT] and bootstrap modeling [CIT].
Much of cheminformatics rests on the similar property principle, which states that structurally similar molecules tend to have similar properties, including biological activity [CIT].
Nearest-neighbor prediction, GP kernels and many noise detection methods rely on it.
Similarity is defined only relative to a representation and a coefficient [CIT].
Two molecules that are near-identical under a substructure fingerprint may be far apart under a PDV, and a computed similarity value is easily over-interpreted [CIT].
The most common measure for binary fingerprints is the Tanimoto coefficient [CIT].
For two molecules with fingerprints x, x' \0,1\^d,
which is the number of bits set in both molecules divided by the number of bits set in either.
Continuous representations are instead compared with a distance, most often the Euclidean distance _j=1^d(x_j - x'_j)^2.
Both measures are sums over the features, and neither weighs a feature by its relation to the property.
In the Tanimoto coefficient, a bit that is off in both molecules contributes nothing, whereas every bit that is set in either molecule counts.
In the Euclidean distance, every feature that differs between the two molecules counts.
Chapter [REF] returns to this point (Equation [REF]).
Distance-based reasoning relies on the assumption that the data embeddings contain quality information.

When the labels are corrupted or the important features are scarce, similarity scores over-rely on compounding false or useless information, and the assumption that similar molecules have similar properties breaks down.
[CIT] found that the Tanimoto, Dice and Cosine coefficients and the Soergel distance rank molecules almost identically on binary fingerprints.
We take this to mean that changing the formula cannot compensate for a weak representation.
This problem is further complicated by activity cliffs (defined below).
These molecules, which potentially contain the most important information for model prediction, can be confused with noise.
Another barrier to distance-based reasoning is persistent noise across labels.
The task of trying to determine if a molecule's value matches that of its neighbors becomes a lot harder when all of the neighbors have some form of noise as well.
There are many downstream tasks which rely on the concept of similarity.
The second half of this thesis relies on many such tasks, and as such focuses on identifying representations that agree with this principle.
An activity cliff is a pair of structurally similar molecules whose potency differs by a large amount because of a small chemical change [CIT].
A cliff also depends on the similarity measure, and there is no widely accepted definition of one [CIT].
The MoleculeACE benchmark [CIT] uses three measures: the Tanimoto coefficient on ECFPs, the Tanimoto coefficient on scaffold fingerprints and a scaled Levenshtein distance on SMILES strings.
A pair counts as highly similar if its similarity exceeds 90\% under at least one of them.
Such a pair forms a cliff if the two molecules also differ tenfold or more in K_i or EC_50 [CIT].
Across the thirty MoleculeACE targets, molecules in at least one cliff pair make up between 7\% and 52\% of a dataset [CIT].
As the number of dimensions grows, the distances to the nearest and to the furthest point become increasingly similar [CIT].
Molecular representations are routinely high-dimensional and sparse.
When many of their features carry no information about the property, distances computed over them are dominated by those features.
Real-world cheminformatics datasets contain label noise arising from multiple sources across the drug discovery pipeline.
Although noise is often modeled as being random, or drawn from a Gaussian distribution, other varieties of noise must be considered when working with experimental data.
To properly model experimental noise, we must first understand where the noise is coming from.

One key issue with QSAR models is the standard ML assumption that labels represent true values, as most chemical datasets lack sufficient replications to provide a robust statistical representation of the underlying distributions [CIT].
A single measurement, or even multiple measurements for a given label, will not guarantee that this label accurately reflects the population mean [CIT].
Most ML models rely on the assumption that the training data is, in fact, an accurate reflection of the population.
Therefore, they treat these potentially noisy labels as discrete quantities rather than distributions, which opens the door to overfitting to noise.
However, Bayesian methods such as Gaussian processes (GPs), and conformal prediction, do not make this assumption [CIT].
Studies involving noise, and specifically the quantification of noise robustness, typically approach label noise by adding independent, zero-mean, Gaussian error to the labels.
However, there's evidence to suggest that noise from experimental assays takes on different forms.

[CIT] rejected normality of the differences in binding affinity between orthologous targets by Anderson--Darling test, found them approximately Laplace, and found that differences between assays of the same ligand and target closely resemble them.

[CIT] examined the widest disagreements among 16,844 pairs of repeat pIC_50 measurements and found that in most cases, the wide gap between repeat values was due to annotation error rather than to an imprecise assay.
Although numerous studies have explored the effects of noise on ML algorithms for molecular property prediction, comparisons between different molecular representations remain limited.

[CIT] examined the predictive limits of QSAR in the presence of noise, showing that by learning the underlying trends rather than fitting to noise, the models can achieve predictions more accurate than those of their training data.

They assumed experimental noise could be modeled as Gaussian-distributed, using the Central Limit Theorem to argue that aggregated experimental measurements from multiple independent error sources exhibit a Gaussian distribution.
However, [CIT] distinguish random noise, which affects all molecules alike, from systematic noise that differs between regions of chemical space.
Using synthetic noise applied only to nitrogen-containing molecules, they showed that mean-variance estimation can detect it.
Beyond just the distribution, the assumptions of independence and zero mean may fail as well [CIT].

[CIT] examined P-glycoprotein transport measurements from 23 laboratories and found that, among the laboratories using cell lines, 62\% of the variance in log digoxin efflux ratio was due to differences between laboratories.
When you pool data from different sources, each source has the potential to carry a shared offset.
These sources usually contain families of related compounds, breaking the independence assumption.
The zero-mean assumption is not assured either, especially when true values fall above or below an assay's detection limit, called censoring.
[CIT] count censored labels in 15 industrial assays, of which 13 carry censored labels and eight sit between a quarter and two thirds censored.
Chapter [REF] tests noise conditions that vary the distribution, the correlation, and the bias of injected error separately, at a matched quantity of noise for every condition except censoring.
Label noise enters bioactivity data at every step from the assay plate to the database.
Table [REF] lists these sources, with examples of each and the kind of error each tends to produce.
The kind of error describes how the error is distributed across molecules, which is the property that the noise conditions in Section [REF] vary.
These noise sources can interact with each other and present in more ways than a simple Gaussian.
Real noise can be heteroscedastic, larger in some regions of chemical space than others [CIT], shared within a laboratory [CIT], and non-normal [CIT].
We wanted to address this complexity in our research by examining a variety of ways of both modeling and adding noise to datasets.

Although the general assumption in much of the noise analysis and mitigation literature is that noise, specifically label noise, will have a negative effect on the model, this is not necessarily the case.
There are multiple instances of using noise as a method of regularization.
In linear regression, appending observations of pure noise shrinks the coefficient estimates, an implicit regularization, although not an optimal one [CIT].
Furthermore, adding artificial noise drawn from a Gaussian distribution to the activation layers of a neural network is considered another form of regularization [CIT].
These studies indicate that the presence of noise may act as a form of regularization in some contexts.
It is important to address this potential of regularization from label noise in QSAR and quantitative structure--property relationship (QSPR) models.

text: As we increased the quantity of noise, we measured how much predictive performance fell.
We explored seven different ways of adding noise, which we refer to as noise conditions and which are illustrated in Figure [REF] and summarized in Table [REF].
Three conditions vary the shape of the distribution from which the error is drawn, and three concentrate the error on some molecules or share it within Bemis--Murcko scaffold families.
The seventh condition, censoring, clips labels at a limit.
The Bemis--Murcko scaffold of a molecule is its ring systems and the chains that link them, with all other side chains removed [CIT].
Molecules that share one scaffold form a scaffold family.
For a given label, every condition except censoring delivers the same expected quantity of noise at a set noise level.
These levels are defined as a fraction of the standard deviation of clean training labels.
The noise added to the label of molecule i is
where is the target standard deviation of the noise, in the units of the label, and z_i is drawn from the condition's distribution at unit scale.

The multiplier s_i is 1 for most molecules and = 3 for those the condition affects, which are a random 10\% of molecules under outlier and whole scaffold families covering 20\% of the split under grouped-wider.
The constant _z is the standard deviation of z, equal to 1 for the Gaussian, /(-2) for the Student-t and 2 for the Laplace.
The factor G divides both of these out, so that has standard deviation in expectation whatever the distribution and whichever molecules are affected.
Grouped-shifted widens no molecule's error, and instead gives every scaffold family g an offset of its own,
with one draw b per family and one draw w per molecule.
The two variances sum to ^2, and the family offset carries a share of that total.
We selected the parameter values from published measurement errors wherever possible, and Table [REF] notes where no published estimate exists.

We found no published estimate of how large a share of a dataset is affected by a difference between laboratories, so under grouped-wider we chose to draw scaffold families until they covered 20\% of the training molecules.
The problem of training a model when some of its labels are wrong is called learning with noisy labels (LNL).
A method that acts on the training data has two halves: what selects the molecules, and what is then done to them (Table [REF]).
A detector infers from the features and labels how wrong each label looks; the score it gives a molecule is that molecule's suspicion score.
A known flag is recorded in the data, such as a label at the assay limit or the molecule's scaffold family.
Noise detection is a detector alone.
Noise mitigation is a selector followed by deletion, down-weighting or moving the label, after which any model can be fitted; Figure [REF] shows how it is evaluated.
Noise-robust training leaves the data untouched and changes the loss, the kernel, a noise term, the training loop or the model, as in co-teaching [CIT] and Meta-Weight-Net [CIT].
A sample-selection step taken out of its training loop and used only to delete molecules before a refit counts as noise mitigation.
[CIT] sort deep learning methods for noisy labels into five groups: robust architectures, robust regularization, robust loss functions, loss adjustment and sample selection.
All five act during training, so all five are noise-robust training.

text: Chapter [REF] tests the principle, and Chapter [REF] tests neighbor-based noise mitigation with the hybrid as the feature space.
The noise conditions are implemented twice.
NoiseInject, an open-source Python package, injects the noise on the three assay datasets of Chapter [REF] and computes the robustness and uncertainty metrics.
QM9 uses a separate Python and Rust pipeline with its own Rust implementation of the same conditions.
Before any cluster run, an automated check compares the two on the same labels, groups and seeds.

Because Rust and NumPy draw different random streams, it compares statistics: the delivered noise, the factor G, the median error, the number of badly corrupted labels and the number of molecules affected.
NoiseInject (version 1.0.0) evaluates model robustness and uncertainty calibration under artificial label noise, for both regression and classification.
It operates on arrays of labels and on the predictions of any externally trained model, which makes it model-agnostic, and its core depends only on NumPy, pandas, SciPy and scikit-learn.
Results are returned as pandas data frames with one row per noise level and one aggregate summary row.
The software is available under an MIT license and archived on Zenodo [CIT].
The regression injector sets a noise shape (Gaussian, Student-t or Laplace) and a targeting rule (uniform, grouped-wider, grouped-shifted, outlier or censoring) separately.
Each named condition is one combination of the two with its parameters, and the name is recorded with every result.
The requested noise is the noise level times the standard deviation of the clean training labels.
The injector solves for the scale / G in closed form (Equation [REF]), and a level of zero returns the labels unchanged.
The affected molecules are selected by a separately seeded random number generator, so they are the same at every noise level while the noise draws change.
Under grouped-wider, whole scaffold families are added in random order until they cover as close as possible to 20\% of the training molecules.
Censoring is parameterized by the fraction f of labels clipped, with its limit at the (1-f) quantile of the clean training labels.
On the training split the censored set is the k = round(fn) largest labels; on any other split it is whichever molecules lie past the training limit.

Each injection also returns a record of the target and delivered root-mean-square noise, the factor G, the solved scale, the mean of , the fraction of molecules affected, the group sizes and the random seeds.
The delivered noise is checked against a band of three standard errors,
where is the delivered root-mean-square noise and is the sample kurtosis of the unscaled draws z, bounded between 3 and 60.
The effective count n_eff is the number of independent contributions the delivered noise averages over, and falls below n when the noise is concentrated on a few molecules.
Under grouped-shifted it is n_eff = (^2/g_eff + (1-)^2/n)^-1, with g_eff = (_g n_g)^2 / _g n_g^2 for family sizes n_g.
At 4 the Student-t distribution has no fourth moment, so the standard error is instead 1.3\,n_eff^\,2/ - 1, with the constant calibrated on the measured spread.
A draw outside the band raises a warning, which a correct injector does on about 1\% of draws; the delivered amount is recorded either way.
A second function returns the noise scale each molecule receives, without drawing noise; we apply it to held-out molecules.
Under uniform and grouped-shifted targeting every molecule gets the same scale.
The package then flags the result as degenerate and does not report a rank correlation of zero.
A separate injector sizes the noise against a unit supplied by the user.
In the KIRBy experiments this unit is the standard deviation of a model's out-of-fold residuals on the clean training labels.
It either adds Gaussian noise, with variance the level times the square of the unit, or shifts 2\%, 5\% or 10\% of labels.
Each shift is the level times the unit, with a random sign or upward only.
It can also add Gaussian noise whose standard deviation follows a per-molecule covariate or a hidden log-normal draw, scaled to the same mean variance.

The package provides six label-flipping strategies: uniform flips, flip rates set by class frequency, asymmetric flip rates for binary tasks, a random flip rate for each sample, a flip rate for each class, and flips directed by a confusion matrix.
Because the realized flip rate usually differs from the nominal probability, a binary search finds the probability that changes a target fraction of labels.
For regression, the package computes R^2, the root mean squared error (RMSE) and the mean absolute error at every noise level.
For classification, it computes accuracy, together with macro- and weighted-averaged precision, recall and F1 score and a per-class breakdown.
Robustness is read from the retention curve ret(x) = m(x)/m(0), where x is the noise level.
Here m is a bounded metric for which higher values are better: R^2 for regression, and accuracy, F1, precision or recall for classification.
The primary summary is the normalized area under this curve, AUCnorm (Equation [REF] in Chapter [REF]), evaluated by the trapezoid rule.
It is the mean fraction of clean performance retained across the noise levels and lies approximately within [0, 1].
It is also less directly correlated with clean-label R^2 than other robustness metrics we tested.
A secondary summary fits ret(x) \!(-(x/_W)^) to the curve.
The shape parameter separates curves that hold and then collapse ( > 1) from curves that fall early and then plateau ( < 1).
The parameter _W sets the scale of the decay, and the fit requires at least four noise levels.

The package also reports the clean baseline and the retention at the highest noise level, flags any curve that falls below zero retention, and can withhold the curve summaries for models whose clean baseline is too low.

For a model that returns a predicted standard deviation u_i for each sample, the package computes, at each noise level, the Spearman correlation between u_i and the absolute error |y_i - y_i|, the empirical coverage 1n_i 1[|y_i - y_i| k u_i] at k = 1 and k = 2, against Gaussian targets of 68.3\% and 95.4\%, the mean interval width 1n_i 2u_i, and the expected calibration error (ECE),
computed over ten equal-count bins B_b of u.
All of these use the clean test labels.
The Spearman correlation between u_i and the injected noise |_i| can only be computed on the corrupted molecules, where the noise is known.
It is reported within each noise level.

A correlation pooled across levels is also returned, but it mostly reflects that uncertainty and noise both rise with the level, so it does not measure whether a model can identify which molecules are corrupted.
Three optional wrappers produce u_i from a point predictor.
The first applies split-conformal prediction to any scikit-learn-compatible model, optionally scaled by the label spread of each molecule's nearest training neighbors.
The second fits an exact Gaussian process with a Tanimoto or RBF kernel through Gauche [CIT], and the third applies Monte Carlo dropout to any PyTorch network [CIT].
Chapter [REF] reports predictive performance as R^2 on held-out molecules and robustness as AUCnorm (Equation [REF]).
Chapters [REF] to [REF] state the metric used for each dataset where it is introduced.
Outside Chapter [REF], results are reported as per-fold scores and their spread across folds, and we use no significance tests.
No split or fold in this thesis is random, and no group of molecules is split between training and test.
Random splitting inflates performance estimates for molecular data, because it places structurally similar molecules on both sides of the train/test boundary [CIT].
For small molecules the group is the Bemis--Murcko scaffold family (Section [REF]).
Section [REF] gives the splits of Chapter [REF], and Section [REF] gives the folds of the later chapters and the groups used for datasets that are not small molecules.
We have introduced both parts of a predictor, the representation and the model.
Similarity depends on the representation and the coefficient, and activity cliffs and uninformative features break the similar property principle.
Real assay noise is often not independent, identically distributed or zero-mean, so we defined seven artificial noise conditions.
Methods for noisy labels fall into noise detection, noise mitigation and noise-robust training, and no single method is expected to win on every dataset.
Our NoiseInject package injects the noise conditions and reports the robustness and uncertainty metrics.
Chapter [REF] asks whether the representation or the model architecture governs how strongly a predictor degrades under label noise, through the questions set out in Chapter [REF].

The work in this chapter is adapted from Punt, A., Hanser, T., Werner, S., and Morris, G.M., NoiseInject: A Benchmarking Framework to Study Noise Robustness in QSAR Models, to be submitted to the Journal of Cheminformatics.
Most of the figures, tables, and text in this chapter are therefore either identical or similar to the content of that manuscript.
The authors' contributions are given in the Statement of Contribution.
In this chapter, we inject the noise conditions of Chapter [REF] into training labels and measure how much predictive performance each pairing of representation and model keeps.

While there have been many investigations into the effect of noise on molecular property prediction, direct comparisons between how different molecular representations respond to label noise remain limited.
The choice of molecular representation certainly affects predictive performance.
[CIT] evaluated 62,820 models and found that fixed representations, in most datasets RDKit 2D descriptors, outperformed representations learned from SMILES and molecular graphs.
Whether these conclusions translate to noise robustness is our question.
Between different types of label noise, [CIT] found no difference in model performance between error distributions with the same mean and standard deviation.
We expand on this by considering alternative patterns of noise, namely noise concentrated in structural groups or on a sparse subset of samples.

This chapter addresses the questions set out in Chapter [REF], specifically how the choice of representation and model architecture explain the variance in predictive performance and in noise robustness, what is the impact of the type of label noise, and whether uncertainty estimates track label noise.

Although we are investigating the effects of label noise stemming from experimental settings, for the purposes of testing we inject controlled amounts of artificial noise into clean labels.

Data were extracted from the QM9 molecular property dataset distributed by PyTorch Geometric [CIT], which contains 130,831 small organic molecules with pre-computed quantum-mechanical properties obtained from density functional theory (DFT) calculations at the B3LYP/6-31G(2df,p) level of theory.
We selected the gap between the highest occupied and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (HOMO--LUMO gap) as the prediction target in QM9.
We assumed that QM9 labels were free of noise, notwithstanding approximations in the level of theory.

Each experiment was replicated 10 times with a distinct random seed and a randomly selected subset of N = 10,000 molecules, split 80/10/10 into 8,000 training, 1,000 validation and 1,000 test molecules.
All models were fitted on those 8,000 training molecules, except the Gaussian processes, which were fitted on a random subset of 5,000 of them; the validation and test molecules were unchanged.
We repeated these experiments on three molecular property datasets with experimentally determined endpoints.
From the OpenADMET initiative [CIT], we used LogD and Caco-2 efflux permeability, with N = 5,039 and N = 2,161 respectively.

We also selected hERG K_i data from ChEMBL [CIT], following a protocol inspired by [CIT]: filter for binding assays, deduplicate by median pChEMBL value, and remove compounds with an inter-assay standard deviation greater than 1.0 log unit, resulting in N = 1,415 compounds.
Each of the three was partitioned into five folds by grouped k-fold cross-validation (CV), and each fold's training block gave up a further grouped fifth as a validation set for early stopping.
A model therefore fits between 3,194 and 3,364 of the 5,039 LogD molecules, depending on the fold, so the Gaussian-process subsample never applies to these datasets.
Unlike QM9's 10 replicates, which are 10 independent draws from one pool, each assay dataset is a single fixed set in which every molecule is tested exactly once and nothing is redrawn.

All splits and CV folds were grouped by the chirality-blind Bemis--Murcko scaffold, implemented such that each distinct acyclic molecule forms its own group, and groups are filled in random order.
Prior to modeling, all molecular structures were sanitized and canonicalized using RDKit to remove invalid valence states and standardize atom and bond typing [CIT].
Prediction targets were standardized to zero mean and unit variance.
Experiments that track uncertainty were run once rather than in replicates.

In this study, we evaluated six molecular representations: extended-connectivity fingerprints of diameter four (ECFP4), Avalon, Sort \& Slice (SNS), physicochemical descriptors (PDV), ChemBERTa and Molecular Hypergraph Grammar GNNs (MHG-GNNs).
The same six were used on QM9 and on the three assay datasets.
ECFP4 is a Morgan fingerprint with radius r = 2 with d = 2048 bits [CIT].
Sort \& Slice takes the same substructures as ECFP4, but it ranks them by prevalence and selects the top L (L=1024) [CIT].
We fitted the Sort \& Slice vocabulary on the training molecules alone, refitting it for each QM9 replicate and for each CV fold.
Avalon is a 2,048-bit fingerprint, generated with the Avalon toolkit through RDKit [CIT].

The PDV representation is a vector of 200 physicochemical descriptors computed with RDKit's MolecularDescriptorCalculator [CIT]; the 200 are listed in Additional file [REF], and the list is fixed in our code rather than taken from RDKit's default descriptor set, which grows between releases.
ChemBERTa embeddings are the mean over the non-padding token embeddings of the DeepChem/ChemBERTa-77M-MTR checkpoint, producing 384 features [CIT].

MHG-GNNs are a GIN-based autoencoder pre-trained on about 1.38 million PubChem molecules using -VAE loss, producing 1024-dimensional embeddings through iterative message passing and found in the published mhggnn\_ pretrained\_ model\_ 0724\_ 2023 checkpoint [CIT].
We z-score normalized PDV, ChemBERTa and MHG-GNN per feature, using the training molecules' mean and standard deviation; ECFP4, Avalon and Sort \& Slice reach the model as built.
To understand model behavior in the presence of label noise, we explored a range of model families.
We fitted tree ensembles, a support vector machine, Gaussian processes and neural networks.
Several are variants of one another, differing in the probabilistic machinery they add, and Additional file [REF] gives every configuration with its settings.
Random Forests (RFs) are one of the most common choices for QSAR modeling thanks to their robustness and interpretability [CIT].
Quantile Regression Forests (QRFs) hold the distribution of training labels in each leaf and compute quantiles over all trees [CIT].
While we used 100 trees for RF, we observed a noisy quantile estimate with 100 trees for QRF, prompting us to use 300 instead.
To observe the effect of the quantile mechanism, we then fit a second RF at 300 trees so the two models were identical in all other settings.
We also used eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) [CIT], Light Gradient-Boosting Machine (LightGBM) [CIT], and Natural Gradient Boosting (NGBoost) [CIT].

NGBoost extends deterministic gradient boosting by treating the parameters of a chosen parametric distribution as regression targets and learns them through boosting with a natural gradient update rule [CIT].
NGBoost relies on scoring off validation data, which differs by dataset.
On QM9 the validation split is already held out of every fit.
However, on the three assay datasets the validation set is a scaffold-grouped fifth of the rows NGBoost is handed, which already exclude the validation molecules.
Support vector machines (SVMs) are a well-established baseline in QSAR modeling [CIT].
We used a radial basis function (RBF) with C = 1.0 and = scale as the kernel, as it accommodates continuous vectors.
Gaussian processes (GPs) are a non-parametric class of models that use a kernel to produce a Gaussian predictive distribution over every data point [CIT].
We fitted three variants of GPs, each with a constant mean and a scaled kernel.
The first uses an RBF kernel and runs on all six representations.
The second uses the Tanimoto kernel [CIT] and was run on ECFP4 alone.
The third is a heteroscedastic variant in which the RBF process is given a second network that predicts the observation noise of each molecule.
One of the major limitations of using GPs in practice is computational scaling; inference has O(N^3) time complexity and O(N^2) memory, where N is the number of training points [CIT].
This can be mitigated with sparse GP approximations, but these introduce approximation error and can be more difficult to tune [CIT].
As such, we used a standard GP and only fit on at most 5,000 training molecules, drawn by a seeded sample.
Due to the size of the datasets, this cap only affected QM9.
We implemented these GP models in GPyTorch [CIT], with the Tanimoto kernel taken from the Gauche framework [CIT].

We tested two deterministic feed-forward architectures, both fully connected and both implemented in PyTorch [CIT]: (i) NN- with two hidden layers of sizes 128 and 64, and dropout after each hidden layer and (ii) NN- with two hidden layers, each of size 128, with dropout applied before the output layer.
Each model was trained using the Adam optimizer with early stopping on validation loss.
We used Bayesian transformations to convert NNs into Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), and implemented them using PyTorch [CIT] with ReLU activations and dropout regularization (p=0.2).
Additional file [REF] gives their full widths, dropout fractions, learning rates and batch size.

The thirteen base models are RF, QRF, XGBoost, LightGBM, NGBoost, SVM, the RBF-kernel GP, and NN, BNN and VBLL in each of the two architectures.

The six variant models are RF (300 trees), the heteroscedastic GP (het.), the Bayesian networks with a variance head, BNN- (var.\ head) and BNN- (var.\ head), and the heteroscedastic VBLL- (het.) and VBLL- (het.).
The seven noise conditions used in this chapter are defined in Section [REF].
We controlled noise quantity using noise levels, representing a fraction of the standard deviation of clean training labels.
We ran experiments across seven levels, 0, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0 and 1.5.
We added the noise to the raw label and standardized the target afterwards, using the clean training mean and spread.

To control the quantity of noise for censoring, we recorded every label above the kth largest clean training label as that limit and used this level as the fraction clipped, at 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5.
Censoring is common in pharmaceutical assays, where a third or more of labels can be censored [CIT].
We ran Gaussian, grouped-wider and grouped-shifted noise on every model and representation pairing.
The remaining four conditions ran on selected pairs.

The Rust program draws the noise for each split separately, in the order its records are stored.
The amount of noise, the censoring limit and the affected scaffold families are all computed from the clean training labels.
Validation labels get the same amount of noise in label units, the same limit and the same families, from an independent draw seeded from the training seed.
The program checks that validation received as much noise as training.
Test labels are never corrupted, but every split records the noise scale each molecule would have received, so that held-out molecules can be scored against the pattern applied in training.
For every molecule, the Rust program records its canonical SMILES, clean and noisy labels, standardized value, injected noise, noise scale and noise pattern.
Each run also writes a summary of the noise parameters and the amount of noise delivered.

The run halts if a record holds a different molecule when it is written than when its noise was drawn, or if any molecule has an all-zero ECFP4 or Avalon fingerprint, which marks a failed featurization.
A self-test mode runs the same noise checks on a label file alone.
Up to this point we have been concerned with how noise affects the predictive performance of QSAR models.
However, label noise should also affect the uncertainty these models report.
Some models return only a point prediction, while others also return an estimate of uncertainty, either as a predicted distribution or as the spread across an ensemble [CIT].
Furthermore, some report a single value of uncertainty while others report one that can be decomposed into an aleatoric and an epistemic component [CIT].
The aleatoric component describes underlying noise the model associates with the data, while the epistemic component represents the uncertainty within the model's fit.
We sought to determine if, as expected, the aleatoric component rises with injected label noise while the epistemic component does not.
For the BNN and VBLL transformations, we took the two components over T = 100 stochastic forward passes [CIT]:
where _t(x) and v_t(x) are the mean and the variance returned for molecule x on pass t, and (x) is the mean over passes.
Here v_t(x) is the predicted observation noise variance.
It varies per molecule in the variance-head and heteroscedastic variants, and is one number for the whole fit in the VBLL transformation.
A full-BNN without a variance head returns no variance, so its uncertainty is epistemic alone.
The other models follow the same split.
For GPs, the epistemic component is the posterior variance of the latent function and the aleatoric component is the learned observation noise [CIT].
All variants of the GP produce one number for the whole fit except heteroscedastic.
For QRF models, each tree holds multiple training molecules.
So for a given molecule, the aleatoric component is the variance of the labels in the molecule's given leaf.
The total aleatoric uncertainty is those variances averaged over the trees.
The epistemic component is the variance of the leaf means across the trees.
NGBoost predicts one variance for each molecule from a single fit, which is aleatoric alone [CIT].
In every model, the total uncertainty is the sum of the aleatoric and epistemic components.
No held-out label carries injected noise, so every comparison against the injected noise was made on training molecules.
Each training set was divided into five folds grouped on Bemis--Murcko scaffolds, and each molecule was scored by a refit that excluded its own fold.
For NGBoost on QM9, three of the five folds were scored to limit its cost.
No uncertainty was calibrated after fitting.
We compute statistics on the held-out molecules, for QM9 the test split and for three assay datasets the held-out fold of the scaffold CV.
Different combinations of dataset, model, representation, noise condition, and noise level are examined in each scenario.
We used the coefficient of determination (R^2) throughout.
For molecule i, let y_i be the clean label, y_i the prediction, _i the noise injected into its label and u_i the predicted uncertainty.
To evaluate the effect of label noise, we tracked predictive performance retention under increasing artificial noise.
For each QSAR pairing we recorded R^2() at each noise level , and normalized it to obtain the retention ratio R^2()/R^2(0).
To quantify robustness, we used the normalized area under this retention curve,
evaluated using the trapezoidal rule over the seven noise levels, \0, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5\, in the units of Equation [REF].
While we tested other metrics of robustness, we found AUCnorm to be less directly correlated to clean-label R^2 predictions.
For censoring, we sweep over a set of fractions to clip the labels prior to normalization.
An AUCnorm value near 1 indicates that the QSAR model in question has retained predictive performance with artificial noise, meaning it is more robust to noise.
Since we normalize the curve by its own clean-label predictive performance, a model with a low clean R^2 has less to lose, so AUCnorm is reported beside clean R^2.
We excluded replicates with a clean R^2 < 0.3 from the robustness analysis (Additional file [REF]), as performance retention ratios become unstable when the clean-label denominator approaches zero.
On QM9 one AUCnorm is computed per replicate, and we report the median over the 10 replicates.
On the three assay datasets one value is computed per scaffold fold, and the median over the five folds is reported.
To compare the relative effect of the 13 base models across datasets and noise conditions, we compared their rankings using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient () between clean R^2 and AUCnorm.

We compared probabilistic models with their deterministic counterparts using a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test paired on the replicate, at = 0.05, separately for each representation and noise condition.
This test was run only on QM9, as with five scaffold folds the smallest attainable p is 0.0625.

We conducted a separate analysis of variance (ANOVA) for each noise condition to identify the relative contributions of molecular representation and model architecture to both predictive performance and noise robustness.
For a given metric y, either R^2 at a noise level of 1.0 or AUCnorm:

where s_r represents the effect of replicate r, _f represents the effect of model family f, _m(f) represents the effect of model architecture m within its family, _j represents the effect of molecular representation j, ()_fj and ()_m(f)j are the interaction terms, and e_fmjr is the residual.
The proportion of variance explained by each term was calculated as the effect size
using Type I (sequential) sums of squares, entered in the order replicate, model family, model architecture within family, molecular representation, interaction.
The 10 QM9 replicates provide the residual.
The uncertainty on each share is the 95\% interval of ^2 over 1,000 bootstrap resamples of whole replicates.
These shares describe the models and representations tested here, not the choice of model or representation in general.
ANOVA relies on the assumption that observations both within and across groups are independent.
Two features of this study break that assumption.

First, each QM9 replicate uses the same data split and the same noise draw for every model and representation, so observations from one replicate are not independent of each other; we therefore entered the replicate as a block.

Second, across the whole set of models in this study, some pairs produced similar predictions that are not independent, so a method present in several near-identical versions would count several times towards the share of model architecture.
To handle this issue, we grouped the models into families.

We considered grouping pairs of models that share a method or an architecture, and compared each pair on clean R^2 and on AUCnorm under the three noise conditions run on every representation, separately on each of the six representations, which gives 24 comparisons per pair.
A pair was grouped when the mean difference between the two models was smaller than their standard deviation across replicates in at least two thirds of these comparisons (Additional file [REF]).

Five families met this criterion: RF with quantile regression forests (QRF; 16 of 24), XGBoost with LightGBM (23 of 24), NN- with BNN- (20 of 24), NN- with BNN- (18 of 24), and VBLL- with VBLL- (20 of 24).

VBLL did not group with the plain or Bayesian network of its own architecture (4 to 10 of 24), as its clean R^2 was lower by 0.02 to 0.09, and NGBoost did not group with XGBoost or LightGBM (2 and 3 of 24).
The two architectures of the plain networks, and of the Bayesian networks, also met the criterion (18 and 17 of 24); we grouped by architecture instead, which the evidence supports equally well.
The 13 base models therefore form eight families.

Within these families, the differences between models accounted for at most 1.0\% of the variance in any outcome and noise condition on QM9, and up to 15.1\% of predictive performance on clean labels on the three assay datasets.
We also ran Tukey's honestly significant difference test between the members of each family, separately for each representation (Additional file [REF]).
With 10 replicates it detects differences smaller than the variation between replicates, so we report it beside the size of each difference rather than use it to form the families.
Across representations, we considered grouping SNS with the ECFP4 fingerprint, as both encode overlapping circular substructure information.
The two differed by more than their variation across replicates on clean R^2 for every model (0 of 13), so all six representations were kept as separate levels (Additional file [REF]).
To assess the interaction between uncertainty estimation and label noise, we posed three questions.
First, whether uncertainty rises with label noise, as measured by the mean u_i over held-out molecules at the highest noise level divided by its value with no added noise, in each replicate or fold.
The second pertains to models that report separate aleatoric and epistemic components.
We divided the increase of mean epistemic uncertainty between the highest level of noise and clean labels by the mean of the aleatoric component to determine how each responds to label noise.
A ratio near 0 means the added noise was attributed to the labels while a ratio of 1 or above means the epistemic component grew as much or more.
We also compared the mean aleatoric component with the standard deviation of the injected noise.

The third question we had was whether per-sample uncertainty values track injected label noise, as measured by the Spearman correlation between u_i and |_i| over out-of-fold training molecules, per fold and per noise level.
We also report the Spearman correlation between u_i and the absolute error of the prediction.

Finally, we asked whether dividing a molecule's out-of-fold absolute error by u_i ranks the corrupted labels better than the error alone, and report the difference between the two Spearman correlations with |_i|.

Considering the two main components of a QSAR model, the molecular representation and the model architecture, we sought to understand how each contributes to both predictive performance and noise robustness.
ANOVA decomposition divides the variance between model family, model architecture within its family, molecular representation, the pairing of the two, the replicate, and a residual.

We ran this decomposition for Gaussian noise, the standard model, as well as methods whose injected noise is related to the feature space, grouped-wider and grouped-shifted (Figure [REF], Table [REF]).
For predictive performance measured in R^2 at a noise level of 1.0, model family and molecular representation account for comparable shares of the variance, 26.6\% and 29.0\% under Gaussian noise.

However, for noise robustness, quantified by the normalized area under the R^2 retention curve (AUCnorm; higher values indicate greater robustness), model family accounts for 47.2\% of the variance while molecular representation for 8.1\%.
This pattern is observed across noise conditions and makes sense, as label noise does not impact the features.

The interaction between model and molecular representation explains 19.9\% of the variance in AUCnorm, more than twice the 8.1\% explained by representation alone, meaning representation acts on noise robustness mainly through the model it is paired with.
As such, we primarily compare representations within each model.
We compare the variance decomposition on both clean and noisy labels (Figure [REF]a).
For predictive performance, the artificial label noise lowers the impact of the choice of model family, while the replicate and residual take more.
This means that the variance is left more up to chance and to the underlying variation within the data itself with label noise, which is the expected behavior.
Robustness divides the variance a bit differently.
Representation explains 8.1\% of the variance in AUCnorm, against 31.1\% of clean R^2, while model family rises to 47.2\%.
The replicate nearly disappears from AUCnorm, likely because each replicate's curve is divided by that replicate's own clean R^2, so a difficult split lowers both and cancels out.
We include two terms which stem from the data rather than the model, the residual and replicate terms.
The replicate measures how much of the variance can be attributed to the train and test split, which in this case is a scaffold split.
On QM9 we replicated each experiment 10 times with different random draws of N=10,000, each time giving a new scaffold split.
On the assay datasets, a replicate refers to one of the five scaffold CV folds.
A large replicate term in ANOVA indicates that the folds differ from one another.
The residual is variance that no other term accounts for.

While we observe similar patterns between noise conditions, the predictive performance of grouped-shifted noise in particular varies significantly between replicates, resulting in a larger share for the replicate.
We find that 28.4\% of the variance in AUCnorm and 51.0\% of the variance in R^2 are due to the replicate, with model family falling to 32.7\% and 8.4\%.
This indicates that the offset applied to each scaffold may account for more of the variance in both R^2 and AUCnorm.
The variance decomposition tells us what aspect of QSAR modeling affects predictive performance and robustness, however it does not tell us about the characteristics of individual models.
All models' performance degrades as the labels get increasingly corrupted with noise (Figure [REF]).
The loss remains small until the artificial noise reaches about half the spread of the clean training labels, and then it begins to drop.
The rate it drops and the quantity of noise retained is not necessarily correlated to the model's predictive performance on clean labels.
Across the 13 base models under Gaussian noise at ECFP4, clean R^2 and AUCnorm rank in opposite directions at a Spearman correlation of -0.10 (p = 0.73) (Figure [REF]).
If anything, the lower a model's predictive performance on clean labels, the less it has to lose as the labels get noisier.
The link between predictive performance and noise robustness can be examined by model family (Figure [REF]).
The forests, boosted trees, SVM, and GP all retain relatively high predictive performance on clean labels while maintaining relatively strong robustness to noise.
The plain NNs and BNNs are among the highest in predictive performance on clean labels, and are the four least robust.
The two variational networks sit between these groups, with lower predictive performance on clean labels and middling noise robustness.
Standard feed-forward networks can make strong predictions under clean labels, however they are not a safe bet under noisy ones.
NGBoost is a standout case in the sense it is highly dependent on its paired molecular representation.
Under Gaussian noise it has the highest AUCnorm on every one of the six representations, yet also the lowest in predictive performance on four of the six representations.
It is one of the worst performing models with respect to R^2 on clean data.
Its high robustness is partially due to the fact that when you start with a low predictive performance, you don't have as much to lose.
However, it maintains shallow robustness curves across representations.
On ECFP4 NGBoost's predictive performance ranks lowest up to a noise level of 0.75 and stays in the lower half at every noise level.
However, on PDV it starts second lowest and ends highest, surpassing the other models between noise levels 1.0 and 1.5.
So when paired with the right features, NGBoost has the potential to make better predictions under higher quantities of label noise.
On grouped-shifted noise, RF has higher AUCnorm values than NGBoost on ECFP4, Avalon and ChemBERTa.
Even then, NGBoost reports the highest noise robustness for PDV, MHG-GNN and Sort \& Slice.
While NGBoost performs well under higher label noise, LightGBM performs well under smaller quantities of noise.
Its performance drops sharply after noise level 1.0.

As we've seen, the choice of representation can have an impact on noise robustness, but that impact is determined by model family, represented by the interaction term between model and representation in Figure [REF].
Some models are more impacted by representation than others, though.
In general, networks span a wider range of AUCnorm across the six representations than any of the other models.
Between ECFP4 and PDV under Gaussian noise, the four plain and Bayesian networks differ by between 0.037 and 0.065 of AUCnorm, while no tree or kernel model shifts by more than 0.011.
VBLLs are an exception, as no two variational networks differ by more than 0.019.
