text: On every dataset the interaction between model and representation explains more of the variance in AUCnorm than representation alone.
To further explore the impact of model architecture on noise robustness, we examined deterministic and probabilistic variants of the same core model architecture.
The hypothesis was that a model that reports a distribution rather than a point value may be more robust to small amounts of injected label noise.
We compared variants across three sets of base models: two NNs labeled NN- and NN- and RF (Figure [REF]).
For each NN, we transform a standard deterministic network into a BNN.
The BNNs with a variance head run at different settings from their Bayesian bases, so they are compared only for uncertainty.
We compared RF to its probabilistic counterpart, QRF, with the same baseline architecture and hyperparameters.
Comparisons of this nature are only possible when the variants carry the same underlying settings (Additional files [REF] and [REF]).
NN- and BNN- therefore share one setting, as do NN- and BNN-, and QRF is compared with a random forest of the same 300 trees (Additional file [REF]).
We compare RF and QRF directly with the same underlying architecture.
QRF had lower AUCnorm on QM9 under Gaussian and grouped-shifted noise on every representation, and changed it little under grouped-wider noise, with almost no change in clean R^2 (Figure [REF]).
On the assay datasets QRF was less robust than RF under grouped-shifted noise on every dataset and representation, and under Gaussian noise on LogD and hERG K_i (Additional file [REF]).
Under grouped-wider noise it was more robust on Caco-2 and mixed elsewhere.

The Bayesian transformations that we used to transform feed-forward deterministic NNs into probabilistic ones produced a slightly larger AUCnorm, but only because they lowered predictive performance on clean labels.
BNN- kept more AUCnorm than NN- in most combinations on every assay dataset, and BNN- on all assay datasets.
On QM9 the Bayesian transformations made no significant change on either predictive performance or AUCnorm for either network.
Until now we've discussed how much predictive capabilities a model is able to retain while its training labels are corrupted with noise.
Now, we consider how confident the model reports its own predictions are in the presence of noise, and whether or not those estimates match the increased label noise.
[CIT] found that the mean predicted uncertainty derived from the GPs increases with the amount of label noise in the training data.
We go beyond the population level and instead ask if a model's per-sample uncertainty tracks label noise.
One key sign that a model is able to handle noise is its ability to track it, represented by the per-sample Spearman correlation between predicted uncertainty and noise magnitude.
As expected, mean predicted uncertainty is positively correlated with Gaussian label noise for most models and representations (Table [REF]).
There are a few exceptions, namely BNN- on PDV and VBLL- (het.) on Avalon for QM9.

BNN- fails to rise in at least one fold on every assay dataset, and both full-BNNs with a variance head fail on MHG-GNN for hERG K_i, and BNN- with a variance head also fails on ChemBERTa and on Caco-2.
[CIT]'s finding therefore holds for almost every probabilistic model on the computed property, and for most of them on measured labels.
While this tells us that the models are reportedly less certain under noisy data, we don't know what the model is attributing this uncertainty to.
To answer this question, we decompose uncertainty estimates into their aleatoric and epistemic components wherever possible.

We expect to see aleatoric uncertainty rise with injected label noise, while the epistemic component should remain relatively constant, as it is the aleatoric component that describes uncertainty in the underlying data.
The models whose frameworks allowed for this decomposition include full-BNNs with a variance head, the heteroscedastic GP, and QRF (Table [REF]).
The two heteroscedastic VBLL networks also report both components, and they separate them more often than any other model, though not on every dataset and representation.
They are not drawn in the figures, as they were not scored out of fold.
The full-BNNs with a variance head behave as expected (Figure [REF]), the epistemic component grows by at most 0.43 of the aleatoric growth in every configuration where the ratio can be computed.

Despite QRF's strong predictive performance and noise robustness, both of its aleatoric and epistemic components rise with noise and on some representations, the epistemic component actually rises at a faster rate.
Unlike the predictive performance and robustness, the representation actually dictates whether decomposition works.
For QRF, the epistemic growth is 0.61 to 1.14 times the aleatoric growth on the three fingerprints, 1.02 to 1.44 times on PDV, and 1.29 to 2.04 times on ChemBERTa and MHG-GNN.

Under Gaussian noise the heteroscedastic GP keeps its epistemic growth below a quarter of its aleatoric growth on PDV, ChemBERTa and MHG-GNN except MHG-GNN on QM9, but not on ECFP4 under grouped-shifted noise, where the two grow by similar amounts.

The noise conditions follow the pattern found in robustness, the three conditions which alternate the noise distribution show similar decompositions to those under Gaussian noise, while grouped-shifted raises the epistemic share of the heteroscedastic GP and of QRF in every pairing of dataset and representation.
This scaffold family-based offset may be appearing as structure in the data rather than label noise to the models.
The aleatoric component indicates that label noise increased, but it doesn't tell us by how much (Figure [REF]).
For each unit of added noise it rises by roughly 0.4 to 1 unit, depending on model, dataset and representation.
The aleatoric component can therefore compare noise between datasets or noise levels, but it does not estimate a dataset's internal error.
Uncertainty estimation breaks under censoring as the process of clipping the labels narrows their spread, which in turn shrinks the total uncertainty.
None of the models tested treat a clipped label as a noisy one, so they actually grow more confident while losing information.
Finally, we ask whether a model's uncertainty on one molecule tracks the noise on that molecule's label.
We assess this using the Spearman correlation between predicted uncertainty and the size of the injected noise over out-of-fold training molecules.
Since Gaussian, Laplace, Student-t and grouped-shifted conditions add noise from the same scale to every label, there is not much for uncertainty to find.

It's the same situation with outlier noise, under which a tenth of the data is chosen at random for extra noise, and with grouped-wider in which each scaffold family falls in a single fold, so a model makes predictions based on unseen scaffolds and has no basis for estimating uncertainty.
The only case where per-sample uncertainty tracking is possible is censoring, as the noise is dependent on the value of the label itself.
The correlations are then large and mostly negative, meaning the model is least uncertain on the labels that were clipped most.

On QM9 with half the labels clipped, on PDV, they run from -0.84 to -0.80 across folds for NGBoost and from -0.47 to -0.41 for the GP, and on LogD with half the labels clipped every fold of every model except the two GPs is at -0.29 or lower.
We divided each molecule's error by its uncertainty and found that the division ranked the clipped labels better than the error alone on QM9 and on most of LogD.
Models are most confident on the clipped labels, probably because the clipping piles many labels into one value, which the model learns to tightly predict.

Ironically, per-molecule uncertainty can be used in reverse to identify clipped labels as the labels a model is more certain about, especially when they fall in a certain range, are most likely to have been clipped.
We investigated how a variety of molecular representations and models perform under increasing label noise.

We used ANOVA variance decomposition across three noise conditions on four datasets to show that molecular representation accounts for a larger share of the variance in predictive performance than in robustness.
Robustness to label noise, as measured by AUCnorm, the normalized area under the R^2 retention curve, is more impacted by the choice of model.
The representation each model is paired with explains more variance than the representation alone.

As such, a representation should not be chosen independently of the model it will be used with, and some models benefit from alternative molecular representations across both predictive performance and noise robustness.
Model family was the primary factor in every decomposition except one, Caco-2 under grouped-shifted noise, where the scaffold fold took the larger share.
Grouped-shifted and censored noise, the two conditions in which the error is systematic, corrupt QSAR model predictions the most.
Changing the shape of the distribution from which noise is drawn barely has an impact on model performance, a conclusion which is in agreement with [CIT].

Low quantities of noise do not make much of an impact, on the HOMO--LUMO gap every base model keeps at least 93\% of its clean R^2 up to a noise level of 0.3, and grouped-shifted noise separates from the other conditions only from a level of 0.75 (Figure [REF]).
Models' performance begins to degrade more rapidly on the assay datasets than on the HOMO--LUMO gap, which makes sense as assay data contain inherent experimental noise.

Tree and kernel models maintained consistent AUCnorm across all representations, while the plain NNs and BNNs depended on the representation they were given, as did the predictive performance of NGBoost.
Across datasets and noise conditions, RF and QRF were reliably robust, although their predictive performance on clean labels was middling and on Caco-2 they struggled under Gaussian noise.
QRF was the slightly less robust of the two, falling below RF under Gaussian and grouped-shifted noise.
Other models performed well only under some conditions.

The GP had the highest predictive performance on clean labels and under independent noise but fell behind when the noise was shared within a scaffold family, NGBoost predicted well only with the right representation, and SVM led in predictive performance under scaffold-shared noise on some datasets.

Transforming a feed-forward network into a Bayesian one increased AUCnorm, but the Bayesian variants never predicted better at any noise level, so switching to a tree-based model is the stronger move under label noise.
With regard to uncertainty estimation, mean predicted uncertainty rose with label noise for almost every probabilistic model on QM9 and for the majority of models on the assay datasets.

Of the models whose aleatoric and epistemic components can be split per molecule, the BNNs with a variance head, the heteroscedastic GP and the heteroscedastic VBLL networks correctly attributed error from the injected noise as aleatoric, while QRF read that error as epistemic.
The success of a split is also dependent on the representation, which is not necessarily the case for predictive performance or noise robustness.

The aleatoric component rises by roughly 0.4 to 1 unit for each unit of noise added, so it can compare noise between datasets or between noise levels, but it does not measure a dataset's internal error.
Outside censoring, no model's per-sample uncertainty identified which labels had been corrupted.
Under censoring the models' most confident predictions are the clipped labels themselves, and dividing a molecule's error by its uncertainty picked out the clipped labels better than the error alone.
QM9 served as a relatively clean baseline as its properties are computed.
The assay datasets containing experimental measurements on the endpoints LogD, Caco-2 [CIT], and hERG K_i [CIT] are smaller and cover a more narrow range of the chemical space.
As the labels in these data are experimentally-derived and pooled from different laboratories, they contain some unknown amount of noise.
We are then adding artificial noise on top of the existing experimental noise.
These validation datasets supported the QM9 findings for the forests, with the boosted trees XGBoost and LightGBM the notable exceptions, degrading on the external datasets.
Future work should extend this type of noise robustness benchmarking to classification tasks and larger experimental datasets with better-known uncertainty estimates.

When training on noisy experimental data in the context of QSAR, it is important to keep in mind that a model's robustness to noise is primarily driven by its own mechanism of training, and to an extent the molecular representation the input data comes in, oftentimes with respect to the model.
Of the models tested, RF was the most consistent choice across the four datasets, ranking between first and eighth for AUCnorm on every dataset, representation and noise condition.
Where a predictive distribution is wanted, its probabilistic counterpart QRF maintains RF's predictive performance and nearly all of its noise robustness.
What QRF cannot do is say where that uncertainty came from.
Beyond the forests, the better choice depends on how much noise there is.
LightGBM and XGBoost predict well on clean labels and lose the most as noise rises, so they suit data you trust, while NGBoost and the VBLL networks start lower and hold what they have.
In this research, we define a noise level as a fraction of the spread of the clean training labels.
It is therefore relative to the dataset rather than an absolute measurement error, and cannot be mapped onto a given dataset exactly.
There are other mechanisms used to estimate the noise in a dataset directly.
When an assay's controls are available, the Z'-factor can be used to estimate noise [CIT].
You can also use screening data to test for row, column and plate effects, which produce systematic rather than independent error [CIT].
When you lack controls, replicates, and metadata, a label can be checked against the data itself.
Confident learning flags labels by comparing each label to what a model predicts for that molecule when it was left out of training [CIT].
You can use the point at which the model error matches the data's error to generate a predictive limit [CIT].
Beyond formal methods, you should consider how a dataset was assembled.
How many independent replicates were done, how many laboratories contributed, whether assay protocols were consistently applied, and how varied are the compounds in chemical space?
The first limitation of this study is data availability.
While HOMO--LUMO gap from QM9 is a good baseline as its computed labels carry no measurement error, it is only a single task.
As the noise is meant to replicate experimental data, this analysis would be improved by more quality-controlled, relatively clean and well-replicated experimental data across different targets.
However, data of that nature are hard to find publicly.
Second, AUCnorm is a ratio to clean R^2, so a model that starts from a low clean baseline has less to lose, and a few replicates scored above 1.05.
We tried other measures of noise robustness, but they were either too strongly correlated with clean R^2 or did not capture the right quantity.
The change in R^2 at a single noise level, for example, misses the shape of the curve.
AUCnorm is not a perfect metric, but it describes the whole curve, and across the 13 base models it is unrelated to clean R^2.
Third, it is hard to draw conclusions that hold across so many conditions.
No model or representation wins everywhere, although RF comes closest.
When working with cheminformatics data, you don't know in advance how a model and representation will perform on the given prediction task.
The underlying data is probably noisy, but you don't know how noisy it is or what shape that noise takes.

Given that, our recommendation is to test a handful of models against a handful of representations rather than tuning a single pairing, since on every dataset the pairing explains more of the variance in robustness than the representation does alone.
The pattern of the noise should also guide that choice (Table [REF]).
The same preferences held on all four datasets.
Under Laplace, Student-t and outlier noise, RF was the most robust model and SVM was the second.
NGBoost lost AUCnorm under all three.
Under grouped-wider noise, QRF was the most robust model and SVM was close behind.
Of the boosted trees, XGBoost lost the most.
Grouped-shifted noise was the hardest condition.
Every model lost AUCnorm on every dataset and representation.
RF lost the least of the models that also predicted well, and the GP lost the most.
Gaussian noise was the only condition with a clear specialist.
NGBoost was the most robust model on the HOMO--LUMO gap under Gaussian noise with every representation, but not on Caco-2 or hERG K_i.
These results follow from the loss function each model fits.
NGBoost fits a per-molecule scale under a Gaussian likelihood, so it loses ground when the noise is not Gaussian.
SVM ignores residuals that fall inside its margin, so it gains under the same conditions.
QRF fits conditional quantiles, so a noisy scaffold family widens that family's interval without shifting the fit.
Each boosting stage fits the residuals of the stage before it, and those residuals are largest in the noisy families.
The GP is the most affected by error that is correlated with structure, because its kernel measures structure.
None of this matters if the data are clean, as little separated the models below a noise level of 0.3.
In this chapter each model was given a standard molecular representation, and the choice of representation explained relatively little of the variance in noise robustness.
We observe that this choice does impact the performance of different models to varying degrees, and the representations seem to capture different signals on each dataset that we tested.
Chapter [REF] asks how well these representations compare molecules on a single dataset.

text: In this chapter we ask if the standard methods of comparing molecules satisfy the SPP, insofar as they do not sufficiently quantify how similar two molecules actually are.
General-purpose molecular representations are designed to work across chemical domains.
Consequently, when considering data from a specific domain, many of their features show little to no variance.
Some representations assign separate molecules identical feature vectors.
Since common fingerprints do not encode stereochemistry [CIT], they are often unable to differentiate stereoisomers, which can have substantially different measured activity [CIT].
As these coefficients compare every feature, irrelevant features dilute the result.
Different representations also disagree about which molecules are close based on the information they carry.

Any method that incorporates similarity measures, such as AC detection, or cleaning a training set by comparing each sample's label with its nearest neighbors' labels, whether by removing the samples that disagree [CIT] or by smoothing their labels, inherits this choice, as do the noise estimation and mitigation methods of this thesis.
[CIT] learn a molecular similarity from graph embeddings, but independently of any endpoint.
[CIT] did choose the similarity for the task.

They predict each molecule's activity as the average over its k most similar molecules by Euclidean distance over descriptors, and choose the descriptors by simulated annealing to maximize the leave-one-out q^2.
[CIT] also optimize the number of neighbors and their weighting.
Both select features for a nearest-neighbor model of one endpoint, whereas this thesis selects features across several representations.
The purpose of this chapter is to establish the problem that Chapter [REF] sets out to solve.
Section [REF] asks, for a given dataset, how much the features of standard representations vary and how many molecules map to identical feature vectors.

Section [REF] asks what happens when these features are used to quantify similarity, and Section [REF] follows the consequences for methods built on these similarity measures, including a small sweep of published noise-handling methods (Section [REF]).

subsection: Distance metrics for continuous molecular descriptors
text: While binary fingerprints are compared with the Tanimoto coefficient (Chapter [REF]), we need distance metrics for continuous feature vectors.

text: The research in Section [REF] used the following four:

subsection: Distance metrics for continuous molecular descriptors
text: Euclidean (L_2): standard geometric distance, d(x, y) = _i (x_i - y_i)^2

subsection: Distance metrics for continuous molecular descriptors
text: Manhattan (L_1): sum of absolute differences, d(x, y) = _i |x_i - y_i|, more robust to outlier features

subsection: Distance metrics for continuous molecular descriptors
text: Cosine: angle-based, d(x, y) = 1 - x y\|x\| \|y\|, invariant to magnitude

subsection: Distance metrics for continuous molecular descriptors
text: Mahalanobis: covariance-adjusted distance, d(x,y)=(x-y)^ S^-1(x-y), where S is the feature covariance estimated on the training molecules [CIT]

subsection: Distance metrics for continuous molecular descriptors
text: All features are standardized to zero mean and unit variance prior to distance computation.

text: The later chapters use a different set, chosen after that study.

text: Like cosine distance, the Minkowski distance with p=0.5 is a dissimilarity rather than a metric, because it breaks the triangle inequality.
General-purpose representations are built to span a broad range of chemical domains.

When your dataset covers only a small region of the chemical space, a lot of the features within these generalized representations become irrelevant, describing chemistry which is absent from the data at hand.
Pairwise comparisons of these representations rely on these irrelevant features.

ECFP4 is the worst offender.
On hERG K_i (1,412 molecules) 1,815 of the 2,048 features are near-constant.
That jumps to 1,997 out of 2,048 near-constant features for the HOMO--LUMO gap on QM9.
292 of MHG-GNN's 1,024 features are zero in every molecule across all seven datasets that used it.
They come directly from the saved encoder output rather than the data, and we have not looked into why.
These constant counts are sometimes filtered out by the distance.
Tanimoto similarity (Equation [REF]; the distance is 1-T) ignores bits off in both molecules, but a bit on in every molecule raises every molecule's measured similarity.
It does not use the 105 constant ECFP4 bits on hERG K_i.
Constant features add zero to a Euclidean or Manhattan distance; however, near-constant features are amplified.
That's great behavior if those features define an AC.
If not, they are contributing disproportionately to the measure of similarity.
A standard fingerprint- or descriptor-based representation can produce the same feature vector for two separate molecules.
In turn, models using this representation will produce a single prediction for the molecules with identical features.
Identical feature vectors do not always mean that the representation has merged two different molecules, since a dataset pooled from several sources can hold two measurements of the same molecule.
Many fingerprints are computed without stereochemistry [CIT].

In this research, ECFP4 is built with stereochemistry off, and the 2D descriptor sets (PDV, Mordred) also ignore it, so almost every molecule they produce identical representations for is a stereoisomer of another (Table [REF]).
Any representation that reads from these subsequently merges stereoisomers.
Additionally, methods using the Weisfeiler--Lehman relabeling scheme are bounded by the 1-Weisfeiler--Lehman test (Chapter [REF]), so some non-isomorphic graphs also receive the same vector.
This is seen in the graph-kernel features which tie 105 of 1,412 hERG K_i molecules, 56 of which differ only in stereochemistry and 49 in more than that.
Whether or not a learned embedding is able to differentiate stereoisomers is dependent on its input as well as its individual implementation.
SMI-TED, a pretrained SMILES encoder, ties 56 hERG K_i, 633 LogD and 177 Caco-2 molecules, all stereoisomers.
A tokenizer can drop stereochemistry prior to training.

The tokenizer of the ChemBERTa-77M-MTR checkpoint (ChemBERTa-2 in Table [REF], called ChemBERTa in Chapter [REF]) gives 72 of the 1,415 hERG K_i molecules of Chapter [REF] the same token sequence as another molecule.
Since stereoisomers can differ in measured activity [CIT], these representations lack potentially useful chemical information.
Two molecules are tied when a representation gives them exactly the same feature vector.
Table [REF] counts ties on hERG K_i, LogD and Caco-2 for each dataset's base representations and augmentation features.
Augmentation features are the small feature sets added to the hybrid after it is built (Section [REF]).
No tie came from one compound listed twice (checked by InChIKey, which differs between stereoisomers) or from a row of zeros.
Apart from the MACCS keys, most tied molecules are stereoisomers.
Atom pairs, PDV, Mordred and SMI-TED tie only stereoisomers, and ECFP4, Avalon and topological torsions add a few molecules that differ in more than their stereochemistry.
On hERG K_i, ECFP4, atom pairs, PDV, Mordred and SMI-TED tie the same 56 molecules, so joining any of these five representations leaves all 56 tied.
The WL graph kernel also ties 49 hERG K_i and 26 Caco-2 molecules that are not stereoisomers, and the MACCS keys tie the most molecules on every dataset, mostly not stereoisomers.
The 3D augmentation features and the learned embeddings ChemBERT, GROVER, MHG-GNN, MoLFormer and GraphMVP tie none, and joining all of a dataset's representations leaves no molecule tied.
A model has to give every molecule in a tied group the same prediction.
The best single prediction for a group is its mean label, so ties set an error that no model can go below,
where n is the number of molecules, G runs over the tied groups and y_G is the mean label of group G.
The matching best R^2 is 1 - RMSE_^2 / Var(y).
On hERG K_i this lowest error is at most 0.134 pK_i (MACCS keys), small next to the label standard deviation of 0.915 pK_i.
Single groups can still disagree by a lot.

Independent pK_i measurements of the same compound against the same target differ by 0.44 log units on average, with a standard deviation of 0.54 [CIT], so a gap larger than 0.54 inside a tied group is larger than typical measurement noise.
On hERG K_i, 6 of the 26 ECFP4 groups and 38 of the 153 MACCS groups differ by more than 0.54.
The widest ECFP4 group is a pair of stereoisomers 1.14 pK_i apart (Figure [REF]).
An ECFP4 model can at best predict their mean, 5.59 pK_i, which leaves each molecule 0.57 pK_i from its measured value.
A tied pair with different labels is also the most extreme activity cliff possible.
The structure--activity landscape index of molecules i and j,
[CIT], is infinite when their similarity is 1 and their labels differ, and here the cliff is made by the representation rather than the chemistry.
A method that judges a label by its nearest neighbors sees a tied neighbor at distance 0 with a different label, and may flag a correct label as noise (Section [REF]).

text: Binary representations were compared by Tanimoto distance, and all others by Manhattan distance on standardized features (Section [REF]), with constant features removed.
Chapter [REF] gives the MoleculeACE definition of an activity cliff, which combines three similarity measures.
Here we use one.
Two molecules are similar if their ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity is at least 0.55 [CIT], and a molecule is a cliff if a similar molecule has a label that differs from its own by more than a set gap.
We chose the gap on each dataset so that 15\% of the molecules are cliffs, so the gap follows the spread of the labels (Table [REF]).
On hERG K_i the gap is 1.76 pK_i, and 211 of the 1,412 molecules are cliffs.
On QM9 only 1,093 pairs of the 9,978 molecules are similar, and the gap is 0.05 eV, 0.06 times the median absolute deviation of the labels.
On the three Biogen datasets (RLM clearance, MDR1--MDCK efflux and HLM clearance) it is 0.20 to 0.34 log units, 0.50 to 0.60 times the median absolute deviation.
The count of cliffs depends on the representation.
We kept each dataset's gap and replaced ECFP4 with each other base representation, calling similar the same number of closest pairs as ECFP4 does.
On hERG K_i the number of cliff molecules then ranges from 138 (atom pairs) to 267 (WL graph kernel).
Of the pairs that ECFP4 calls similar, only 57\% to 74\% are also among another representation's closest pairs, and on QM9 only 1\% to 24\% (Additional file [REF]).
We asked whether distance tracks label difference in two ways.

Over all pairs of molecules, we took the Spearman correlation between the distance of a pair and the absolute difference of its labels, a one-number summary of the neighborhood-behavior plot of [CIT]; datasets above 2,000 molecules were sampled down to 2,000.

Over each molecule's closest pairs only, we predicted each label as the mean label of the molecule's five nearest neighbors, taken from other scaffold groups, and took the Spearman correlation between predicted and measured labels.
Across the 70 combinations of dataset and representation, the all-pairs correlation ranged from -0.04 to 0.23 and was below 0.10 in 44 of them.
The five-neighbor prediction reached 0.29 to 0.89, higher than the all-pairs correlation in all 70 (Table [REF]; every representation is in Additional file [REF]).
On hERG K_i with ECFP4, the all-pairs correlation is 0.06, while the five-neighbor prediction reaches 0.72, with an RMSE of 0.63 pK_i against a label standard deviation of 0.92 pK_i.
Figure [REF] shows why the two differ.
Of the 996,166 hERG K_i pairs, 93\% have an ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity below 0.20, and only 1.1\% reach 0.55.
Over all pairs the median label difference is 0.81 pK_i, but above a similarity of about 0.4 it is 0.20 to 0.30 pK_i, although 8.3\% of the 774 pairs at 0.8 or above still differ by more than 1 pK_i.
Mordred shows the same pattern: the closest 5\% of pairs have a median difference of 0.44 pK_i, and every other 5\% has 0.78 to 1.11 pK_i.
The useful information sits in the few closest pairs.
The all-pairs correlation is set by the other 95\%, whereas the five-neighbor prediction uses only the closest pairs.

We compared the five nearest neighbors of each molecule, from other scaffold groups, under ECFP4, SMI-TED and Mordred (PDV on Caco-2, where Mordred is not a base representation; on HLM clearance ECFP4 is not a base representation and its stored features were used).
On hERG K_i any two of the three share on average 0.47 to 0.52 of each molecule's five neighbors, and on the three Biogen datasets and QM9 only 0.13 to 0.21 (Table [REF]).
For 500 random pairs per dataset we found the maximum common substructure (MCS) with RDKit [CIT], allowing 2 seconds per pair and leaving out pairs that ran out of time.
The MCS distance is 1 - n/(a+b-n), where n is the number of atoms in the common substructure and a and b are the numbers of heavy atoms in the two molecules.
Its Spearman correlation with ECFP4 Tanimoto distance ranged from 0.20 (hERG K_i and HLM clearance) to 0.51 (Caco-2 and LogD).
Every method in Section [REF] takes a similarity as input and inherits the dilution described here.

text: We sought to address the second with the adaptive hybrid representation (Chapter [REF]), which concatenates the top-ranked features by importance from several base representations.
Neighbor-based noise detection treats a label far from its neighbors' labels as probably wrong, an idea that goes back to editing nearest-neighbor training sets [CIT].
The wider literature on filtering noisy labels concerns classification [CIT].
[CIT] adapt fourteen classification noise filters to regression, seven of them nearest-neighbor filters that use the neighbors' mean label.
They find that the filters improve regression methods on 20 general regression benchmarks with injected label noise, none of them QSAR datasets.
The neighbor-based noise scores, sample removal, sample weighting, label smoothing and the recovery rate are defined in Chapter [REF] (Sections [REF] and [REF], Equation [REF]).
The method needs a distance that picks the right neighbors, and neighbors with clean labels.
Earlier sections of this chapter argue that the first condition fails, and the second fails whenever noise is spread over the whole training set.
A large gap from the neighbors' labels can mean a noisy label, a noisy neighbor or the wrong neighbors, and the score cannot tell which.
Activity cliffs also look like noise to such a detector (Chapter [REF], ``Molecular similarity and activity cliffs'').

With the neighbor-based scores used as sample weights at strength = 0.1, mean recovery was negative for every representation at both noise levels (Table [REF]).
Of all 860 cleaning configurations, 8 had positive recovery at both noise levels; 6 of these used a single representation, and 4 of those 6 were neighbor-based.
Label smoothing toward neighbor or model estimates gave positive recovery in 5.0\% of configurations at = 0.3 and 0.8\% at = 0.6.
Mean recovery was negative at every weighting and smoothing strength tried, from 0.1 to 0.7.
Judging a label by its neighbors usually made the model worse and rarely helped at both noise levels, but it did not always fail.
The best configuration at = 0.6 was neighbor-based (PDV, Euclidean distance, local variance ratio score) and recovered +17.2\%.
Because noise was added to every training label, the neighbors' labels are noisy too; the exploratory study gave this as the reason label smoothing failed.
Uncertainty-based methods, which use no neighbors, showed potential at lower noise but degraded at higher noise.
Sample weighting did better than label smoothing but usually still hurt, with positive recovery in 14.2\% of configurations at = 0.3 and 4.7\% at = 0.6, and mean recoveries of -22.9\% and -20.9\%.
The study also found neighbors in an early hybrid of 100 PDV and MHG-GNN features, built by greedy forward selection, which is no longer part of the method.
Its mean recovery with neighbor-based scores was -0.9\% at = 0.3 and -3.0\% at = 0.6, with 44.4\% and 27.8\% of configurations positive.
On a single dataset, often very little of a standard representation varies.
On hERG K_i, 1,815 of the 2,048 ECFP4 features take one value in at least 95\% of the 1,412 molecules (Section [REF]).
Several representations also give different molecules, mostly stereoisomers, the same feature vector, and no model can separate those molecules, whatever their labels.
ECFP4 gives 56 of the 1,412 hERG K_i molecules a vector shared with another molecule, all of them stereoisomers (``Molecules with identical feature vectors'').
A distance sums over every feature, so when only a few features matter for the property, the rest dominate the sum (Section [REF]).
Across 70 combinations of dataset and representation, the Spearman correlation between pair distance and label difference was below 0.10 in 44.
Predicting each label from its five nearest neighbors gave a higher Spearman correlation in all 70, so the useful information sits in a few close pairs rather than in the distance as a whole.
We found that methods built on a distance did worst under label noise.
In the small sweep of published noise-handling methods, the configurations with the lowest retention all used a distance (Section [REF]).
Judging a label by its neighbors' labels usually made the model worse (Section [REF]).
Chapter [REF] tests neighbor-based detection under other noise conditions.
A representation that avoids these flaws would need five properties (Table [REF]).
Its features would be chosen for the task, using only each fold's training labels.
It would be compact, dropping features that do not vary or do not matter, with the number kept searched rather than fixed.
It would draw on several representations, since each misses information the others capture; plain concatenation does this but is not compact (Chapter [REF], ``Combining representations'').
It would work both as a model input and as a space for similarity.
Finally, it would be traceable: each chosen feature leads back to its representation and can be read chemically wherever the base feature can.
Feature selection cannot fix every flaw.
Molecules identical in every base representation stay identical in the hybrid, and a selected hashed bit still merges every substructure folded into it.
Selection also needs enough labeled molecules to estimate which features matter.
We tested the published methods and the neighbor-based cleaning on one dataset, the QM9 HOMO--LUMO gap, with Gaussian noise on every training label.
Each molecule's neighbors were therefore noisy too.
The sweep also added a distance to methods designed without one, so poor adaptation may explain part of their result.
Chapter [REF] builds the adaptive hybrid representation and asks how to select its features for a given prediction task (Section [REF]).

Most research in this field relies on a single representation, and few combine features from different representations beyond concatenation.
One of the reasons just pooling features from different representations together doesn't work is dimensionality.

If you add a standard ECFP4 (d=2,048) with Mordred descriptors (d=1,613) and an MHG-GNN embedding (d=1,024), you end up with 4,685 features, which is far too many considering many datasets from experimental assays contain only a few hundred labeled samples.
With such ratios, more features mean weaker predictions [CIT].
Therefore, we consider ways of combining representations.

Other methods handle training on several representations or on too many features.
Ensembling, a form of late fusion, fits one model per representation and aggregates their predictions, so the representations are combined after training.
Consensus QSAR works this way [CIT].
No model in an ensemble sees features from another representation, so it cannot use their interactions, and every representation and model is computed for each new molecule.
When you want to filter a feature set for the features most important to the prediction task, you can use a dimensionality reduction technique or feature selection methodology.
Principal component analysis (PCA) uses linear combinations of the original features, ordered by the variance they explain [CIT].

Their combined features are dependent on the original feature units unless each feature is z-scored first which matters when data from different modalities like fingerprint bits, descriptors and embeddings are joined [CIT].
PCA never sees the labels, and components with small variance can still be important in prediction [CIT].
Partial least squares (PLS), the supervised counterpart in chemometrics, builds components that covary with the property [CIT].
Neither gives components that can be traced to one substructure, descriptor or representation, making them difficult to interpret.

When selecting features, the question is not only what features are most important, but also, what features does the model prefer?
One of the ways to answer this is to consider how many features relative to the size of a dataset a given model works best with.

Distance-based models such as k-nearest neighbors (kNN) and SVM use every feature in every distance computation (Chapter [REF]), whereas tree ensembles choose one feature per split and can essentially ignore irrelevant ones.
[CIT], who created a substructure-based fingerprint called Sort \& Slice, suggest that using labels to select features may result in overfitting.
Table [REF] compares these alternatives with the adaptive hybrid methodology developed in this thesis.
The task of selecting the best features from a set of representations and combining them is not simple.
How do you measure what features are ``best''?
Are these features ``best'' relative to the representation they came from or to the whole pool of features?
Should you select more features from representations that seem to have more signal to begin with, or take a set number of features from every representation?
How many base representations should you select features from?
How many features should you select?
When scoring potential combinations of features, what type of evaluator should you use?
In a dream world, there would be a single answer to each one of these questions that applies to every dataset.

Unfortunately we live in reality, and as I discovered, the answer to every single one of these questions is ``depends on the data.'' The task of selecting the best features then became a search space optimization challenge.
The question actually became for a given prediction task, defined by the dataset, prediction target, and model, what is the best methodology for selecting features?
The hybrid search does not output just a list of features, rather it outputs an ideal search configuration to find features for your data.
It tells you how to score features (feature importance score), what rules you should use to select them (allocation method), how to score potential hybrid feature combinations (internal evaluator).
In this research, I run this hybrid search multiple times across different maximum number of features (budgets), number of input representations, and models (downstream evaluators) on each dataset.
While it is not formal ``training'' in the ML sense, the hybrid search is essentially a feature selection method that is fit on the training data.

text: Because only original features are kept, each traces back to one representation, which makes blueprints possible.
As explained above, the adaptive hybrid representation relies on a search.
A completed search is saved as a blueprint, which records the settings needed to select the features that make the hybrid representation.
Because each selected feature traces back to its original base representation and relative importance rank, the search can tell you about your own prediction task.
The best configuration is saved for each downstream model and budget, giving one blueprint per pair, allowing us to compare blueprints and see if different models prefer different features.
Depending on the origin of the feature, some are chemically interpretable.
By definition, the PDV contains values that relate back to chemical properties like molecular weight or logP.
An ECFP4 bit can be shown as the atom environment that sets it, and a MACCS key stands for a known substructure.
Beyond small molecules, the readable unit of an antibody is a sequence position and its residue.
This feature-level explainability fails when features are derived from learned embeddings.
That will only tell you if the learned embedding itself is useful as a representation, but nothing about the selected feature.

While a set of thousands of features may seem overwhelming and irrelevant, identifying substructures or descriptors that recur among the selected features can point to parts of the molecule that may be involved in binding or activity.
If the selected features make sense chemically for that endpoint, it's a good sign that the selection mechanism is finding real signal instead of fitting noise.

Conversely, if the hybrid search is done over a range of budgets or models, and the blueprints are showing a vastly different set of features, that may be an indication that the features at hand are struggling to provide information about the prediction task.
A predictor that scores proposed molecules in generative design [CIT] could also take a hybrid as input, which we leave to future work.

The hybrid search is a generalized search that takes in multiple feature matrices from the same samples and a supervised prediction task, and outputs a feature selection method that produces a filtered set of features from those original vectors.
The default search objective scores prediction only, meaning the methodology applies to tabular tasks or cases where you have different measurements of the same inputs.
Although this was developed with small molecules and QSAR modeling in mind, it is by no means limited to that use case.

While there are some functionalities in this research that are tailored to chemical tasks, such as blueprints mapping features back to their chemical interpretations and the use of nearest-neighbor objectives (Chapter [REF]) to aid in the computation of molecular similarity, the core functionality of the hybrid process is domain-independent.
One caveat concerns sparse representations such as one-hot encoded sequences.
Each of their features is set in only a few samples, so each scores low importance on its own.
Here, the one-hot encoding is a base representation on three antibody datasets: nanobody thermostability, change in binding free energy ( G) and CHO polyreactivity.
The blocks substitution matrix (BLOSUM) encoding is a base representation on humanness.

text: Six settings in total are searched, namely the downstream model, the budget, the representation count, the importance method, the allocation method and the internal evaluator.

marker_lines: % TODO: manual review -- fixed: table description updated; that table no longer has speed tiers
text: Table [REF] gives the values each setting can take, and Table [REF] the smaller set searched on each dataset in this chapter (Section [REF]).

marker_lines: % TODO: manual review -- fixed: table description updated; that table no longer has speed tiers
text: The importance methods tested are LightGBM gain, TreeSHAP or DeepLIFT (Section [REF]).

marker_lines: % TODO: manual review -- fixed: table description updated; that table no longer has speed tiers
text: Feature-level importance depends on the model as well as on the data [CIT], and as such we observe that within the search, a different ranking of features produces a different hybrid output.
The downstream model is trained on the hybrid representation.
This model can be a supervised model of any form, classification or regression.
We used random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, SVM, a deep neural network (DNN) and a Gaussian process.
Each dataset in this chapter uses two of them (Section [REF]).
The budget is the maximum number of features in the hybrid, taken from eight values (10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1,000 and 2,000 features).
When the budget is too small, informative features can be left out, yet when it is too large it will pick up on too many uninformative ones, especially ones that give small datasets room to overfit.
On nanobody thermostability the search picked 1,000 features for the DNN on four of five folds, and 250 or 500 for the SVM (Figure [REF]).
We select a set of up to 10 base representations per dataset, chosen prior to the search (Table [REF]).
The selections were made based on each representation's relative performance on the prediction task.
We took into account what type of information each representation contained, and tried to span a wide set across the selected 10.

For example, while there are many high-performing graph-based embeddings in QSAR modeling, for the purposes of testing a feature selection process which takes features from different sources of information, it is better to have a mix of graph-based embeddings, as well as other types of molecular representations like substructure fingerprints, property vectors, sequential embeddings, etc.
The representation count (2, 3, 5 or all) sets how many may contribute features, keeping those with the highest standalone scores on each fold.

The number of representation counts to test is searched in the sweep as datasets differ in how many representations have features worth selecting, and pooled feature selection over all representations has no such setting.

While we tested various methods of pooling the features, we found computing feature importance scores and concatenation techniques on a global pooled feature set was far less effective than when the feature scoring is kept on a per-representation basis.
Since the features contain different types of information at different scales, pooling the features too early makes comparisons within the pool challenging.
We found that it's better to determine which features are important to each representation first, and go from there.
Every allocation method is paired with every count.
In preliminary runs, some datasets performed best with 2 or 3 representations and others with all 10.
The full runs show the same split.
On LogD, counts of 2, 3, 5 and all were searched.
The hybrid used all 10 representations on nine of the ten folds, five for each of the two downstream models.
On QM9 with LightGBM, which searched 3 and all, it used 3 on every fold.
We run a feature importance scoring method on each base representation, which gives each feature a single positive score.
These scores remain relative within a given representation, so they are not compared or normalized between representations.
Split-based tree importance is biased toward features with many possible split points [CIT], which matters here because we use binary fingerprint bits alongside continuous embeddings.
No single importance method works best across datasets and downstream models.

After testing a wider variety of methods found across literature, we settled on three methods whose rankings did not correlate strongly with each other and whose selected features performed well as model input (Additional file [REF]).
We score features using LightGBM gain importance, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values for tree ensembles (TreeSHAP) and DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) [CIT].
LightGBM gain measures how much a feature reduced the training loss where trees split on it [CIT].
TreeSHAP gives each feature's exact Shapley value for each molecule's prediction from a tree model [CIT].

DeepLIFT measures how much a feature moves the output of a small network, trained with Adam [CIT], away from its output on an all-zero reference input, which after standardization places every feature at its training mean [CIT].
On Caco-2, the median share of features scoring above 0 was 30\% for LightGBM gain, 70\% for TreeSHAP and 90\% for DeepLIFT (preliminary, over 10 representations and 3 folds).
Table [REF] gives the settings of each method, including the pre-screen of representations wider than 2,000 features.
Each dataset searches one, two or all three importance methods depending on its individually-decided search settings (Table [REF]).
The allocation method decides how many of the B features each representation contributes while the importance method decides which.
Of the five methods searched, four give each representation a fixed share computed from its rescaled standalone score (linear, squared, softmax and rank-decay allocation).
The fifth, the global pool, lets the candidate features offered by every representation compete in one importance ranking.

text: We therefore removed it from the search (Additional file [REF]).
The fixed-share methods differ only in how w_k is computed from r_k (Table [REF]; worked example in Table [REF]), with settings fixed for every dataset.
Every rescaled score lies between 0 and 1, so softmax cannot give one representation most of the budget: with 10 representations the best takes at most 23.2\%.
Rank decay uses only the order, so with 10 representations the best receives 27.3\% and the tenth 1.8\%, whatever the gaps between their scores.
The global pool sizes each representation's offer with squared weights r_k^\,2, as shares of a pool of 2B candidate features.
Each offer is capped at the representation's width and holds only features scoring above 0.
The same importance method is fitted once on the joined offers, and the hybrid keeps the top B features that score above 0.
Each representation's count is therefore an outcome of the joint ranking, with no minimum of one feature, and a feature's rank depends on what the other representations offered.

text: Each internal evaluator is fitted on the internal training fold and scores on the internal validation fold within that CV iteration using the dataset's specified evaluation metric.
A random forest, LightGBM or DNN downstream model is searched with three internal evaluators, because its matched evaluator is already one of the other three.
An XGBoost, SVM or Gaussian process downstream model is searched with four, because the matched evaluator adds one of its own family.
Only the DNN evaluator shares its downstream model's architecture and training settings.
Even it draws its 20\% early-stopping samples at random, whereas the downstream DNN splits them by the outer split's groups.
Additional file [REF] gives every evaluator setting.
The internal evaluator's scores determine how the budget is split and which representations are kept.
The internal evaluator ranks candidate feature sets, it explicitly does not rank features within a representation.
This process of selecting a feature set by fitting a model on it, and keeping the set that scores the best is known as the wrapper method [CIT].
This is distinct from a filter method which scores features without fitting a model.
The search tests every combination of the six settings on a dataset under 5-fold cross-validation.
Over every value of Table [REF], this is 8,160 configurations with five downstream models.
With each dataset's own values, the searches reported in this chapter scored 108 to 3,360 configurations per outer fold (Table [REF]).
Each dataset's grid is a small cut of the full search, made to save compute (Section [REF]).
At worst, a smaller grid finds a less informative hybrid than the full search would have.
Before the full runs, we ran preliminary design experiments on 1 to 9 datasets to choose the values each setting may take (Additional file [REF]).
A value was kept if it gave the best score for some dataset, downstream model and budget.
A setting was fixed at one value when the spread between its values was smaller than the spread of one value across folds.
On hERG K_i, for example, five ways of rescaling each representation's score differed by less than one of them varied across folds, so the rescaling is one fixed rule per metric.
Some feature sets are too small or too specialized to take part in budget allocation, such as MACCS fingerprints (167 features) or log-likelihood ratios (3 features).
Others, such as mutation features that record differences from a parent antibody, carry meaning only beside a full representation.
They cannot contribute many features, so including them would distort the budget split.
We therefore add them as augmentation, calling the finished hybrid H the base and the feature sets that supply extra features the donors.
Donors are set per dataset (Augmentation column of Table [REF]).
On QM9 the topological torsion fingerprint (2,048 features) is the only wide donor.
[CIT] reported that combining 2D and 3D descriptors gave many more significant models across six protein--ligand series (461 structures), which they attribute to complementary properties.
Their 3D descriptors came from bioactive conformations in the Protein Data Bank, whereas our 3D donors use one generated conformer per molecule.
Donor features are ranked by what the base gets wrong.
Inside each outer training fold, an 80/20 internal split keeps each scaffold family or sequence group on one side.
A small random forest (50 trees, depth at most 10) is fitted on the base features.
Three-fold group-aware cross-validation gives out-of-fold residuals r_i = y_i - y^oof_i for the internal-training samples.
For binary tasks, y is the positive-class probability.
In-sample residuals would shrink toward zero.
All donor features are pooled, each is scored by its absolute Pearson correlation with the residuals, c_j = |_P(x_j, r)|, and the top M = 50 go forward.
Ranking against y would favor features that repeat what the base captures.
Ranking against r favors features that explain its errors, as in gradient boosting [CIT] and least angle regression [CIT].
Blocks of the top k \0, 5, 10, 20, 40\ ranked features, capped at the number of candidates, are each added to the base.
Each is scored with the downstream model on the internal-validation samples.
The chosen k^* has the best score, and k=0 wins ties, so keeping no extras is the default.
Five block choices instead of about 50 accept-or-reject decisions leave less room to overfit a small validation set [CIT].
The chosen donors and feature positions are stored and re-extracted for the outer fold.
In uncapped mode, extras are appended outside the budget, so the final width is |H| + k^*, at most B + 40 features.
In capped mode, they replace the base features with the lowest random forest importance, so the width stays at most B.
Uncapped augmentation and no augmentation differ in width at the same B, so their comparison mixes better features with more features.
Capped mode removes this difference, since each extra replaces a base feature.
Augmentation is not a searched setting.
A dataset with donors is searched three times, with no, uncapped and capped augmentation (Table [REF]).
An earlier search of each whole dataset covered 16 datasets of an earlier list.
On none did either augmented condition beat no augmentation by more than 1\% (3\% on datasets under about 1,000 samples).
The searches in this chapter therefore run without augmentation on all 20 datasets (Section [REF]).
Only the nearest-neighbor search on SMAC colloidal stability and HIC retention keeps uncapped augmentation (Chapter [REF]).
The residual ranking has four limitations. |_P| captures only linear relations, one feature at a time.
It ignores redundancy, so two near-identical donor features can both rank high.
Donors are pooled with no per-donor limit, so a 2,048-feature donor gets more chances than a 49-feature one.
Finally, the margin over k=0 is zero, so a near-tie on one internal split can admit extras.
Searching every value of Table [REF] in every fold of every dataset was too slow, so each dataset searches a smaller grid (Table [REF]).
From an earlier search of each whole dataset, we kept the two downstream models with the best scores.
We also kept the budgets whose ten best configurations scored within 1\% of the best budget (3\% on datasets under about 1,000 samples), widened to at least three consecutive budgets.
Importance methods, allocation methods, internal evaluators and representation counts that scored well below the best were dropped.
Two datasets, QM9 and hERG blocking, were too slow for the earlier search over every value.
They were searched over a shorter fixed list, called the fast tier (LightGBM gain importance; linear, squared and rank-decay allocation; three or all representations), and their grid stays within it.
The search with the nearest-neighbor objective has its own grid, given in Chapter [REF].
Table [REF] follows one dataset, hERG K_i, through the cuts.
Its earlier search, without augmentation, covered six downstream models including kNN.
The best had an RMSE of 0.547 pK_i (SVM, 1,000 features, LightGBM gain, softmax allocation, random forest evaluator, all representations).
Its standard deviation over the five folds was 0.044 pK_i.
Most of the fitting time removed by keeping only the SVM and the DNN came from XGBoost (35\%) and LightGBM (25\%).
For each later cut, the best configuration it removed was behind the best kept by less than the spread over folds.
The final grid still contains the best configuration, which is expected, because the cuts were chosen on this same search.
The search also has an adaptive pruning option.
We did not use it, because the per-dataset cuts above remove far more configurations.
It scores every configuration on two of the five folds and stops scoring those far behind, as successive halving [CIT] and Hyperband [CIT] do.
Every experiment splits each dataset into outer folds as set out in Section [REF].
The search sees only the training samples of each outer fold, and the selected features are rebuilt on them and applied unchanged to the held-out samples.
Three experiments also limit each held-out feature to the range it takes on the training samples.
They are the comparison with the best single representation, the easy and hard halves, and the comparison of many and few representations.
The other experiments do not limit held-out features.
Because of time and computational constraints, not every experiment in Chapters [REF] to [REF] ran on every fold or every dataset.
Some experiments here ran on the first three outer folds, most noise experiments in Chapter [REF] ran on the first outer fold only, and some runs had not finished when this thesis was written.
We report the results that exist, give the number of folds beside each one, and name the datasets where a result is missing.
We do not repeat this caveat at every result.
The hybrid is compared with the best single base representation at its full number of features, which is what a user would otherwise run.
This comparator is chosen per downstream model and per fold from the search's scores on the outer training samples.
It is then refit on those samples and scored on the same held-out samples as the hybrid, so it can differ between folds.
The hybrid is held to its budget, so the comparator is often many times wider.
Both widths are recorded for every fold, since a difference between the two scores is partly a difference in width.
The main quantity per fold is the hybrid's score minus that of the best single representation, signed so that a positive value means the hybrid scored better (for RMSE the sign is flipped).
The hybrid experiments use 20 datasets (Table [REF]): seven of small molecules, 12 of antibodies and one of reactions.
Their curation is given in Additional file [REF] and their representations in Table [REF].
Antibody datasets outnumber small-molecule ones, but small molecules are the focus of this chapter, and results are read per dataset, not pooled across a domain.
Additional file [REF] gives the shared and per-dataset pre-processing steps, with the counts after each step.
The LogD and Caco-2 labels are clipped at their 1st and 99th percentiles, so on Caco-2, for example, 22 molecules share the highest label and 23 the lowest.
As in Chapter [REF] (Section [REF]), no group is split between folds.
Classification folds are also stratified with a fixed seed.
Every dataset uses five outer folds, and no split is random (Section [REF]).
On a given dataset, every representation, model and hybrid is scored on the same folds.
The small-molecule datasets, QM9 included, are grouped by Bemis--Murcko scaffold (Section [REF]), here keeping stereochemistry.
On QM9 the largest group is the empty scaffold of acyclic molecules, with 1,041 of the 9,978 molecules.

The two datasets from Biogen [CIT] (rat microsomal clearance and MDR1--MDCK efflux) have 1.2 and 1.1 molecules per scaffold, respectively, so holding out a scaffold there is close to holding out single molecules.
Chapter [REF] used a different scaffold key and different curation for its versions of LogD, Caco-2, hERG K_i and QM9, and Additional file [REF] lists the differences.
The reaction dataset is Buchwald--Hartwig C--N couplings from high-throughput plates.
Following [CIT], it is grouped by additive, so each held-out fold holds four or five additives unseen in training (Additional file [REF]).
In the Koenig deep mutational scan of the anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) antibody G6, each variant carries one mutation.

Variants are grouped by their mutated position, giving 225 groups, so all mutations at one position fall on the same side of a split and a model cannot look up a per-position effect at test time [CIT].
The nanobody and humanness sets are grouped by single-linkage clusters at 95\% sequence identity, the identity threshold [CIT] used to cluster their pretraining sequences.
The two AbAgym deep mutational scans (EGFR and angiopoietin-2 binding) are grouped by mutated position, as for the Koenig scans, giving 36 and 20 groups.
The G set joins antibody--antigen entries from SKEMPI 2.0 and AB-Bind.
It is grouped by protein complex, giving 30 groups, so no complex is on both sides of a split.
The five Ginkgo developability assays are measured on the same panel of antibodies.
Two are retention times, in hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC) and standup monolayer adsorption chromatography (SMAC).
The others are affinity-capture self-interaction nanoparticle spectroscopy (AC-SINS), expression titer, and polyreactivity to Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cell proteins.
We use the five cross-validation folds released with the competition [CIT] as the groups, so their outer folds are the competition's folds.
Some groupings give very unequal folds.
The Ginkgo competition folds hold 35 to 53 antibodies.
Per-fold scores on these datasets spread more widely.
Any representation that gives one fixed-length vector per sample can serve as a base representation (Section [REF]).
The first version of the method used three molecular representations: PDV, ECFP4 and MHG-GNN.
These three are now one small-molecule example among many.
Every base representation is frozen: it is computed once from the raw input (a SMILES string, a sequence or a reaction) and is never trained on the labels.
To choose them, every candidate representation was first scored on its own with a gradient-boosted tree model [CIT] under the dataset's grouped folds.
Candidates were then compared by the Spearman correlation between their out-of-fold predictions, since two representations whose predictions correlate highly carry much the same signal.
At most ten were then chosen by hand, looking at each candidate's own score next to these correlations and favoring representations that encode the input in different ways.
Binding free energy has eight.
Which representation is best depends on the downstream model as well as the dataset.
The best one is the same under both of a dataset's downstream models on three of the seven small-molecule datasets and five of the twelve antibody datasets (Table [REF]).
On hERG K_i, for example, MHG-GNN is best with the SVM and GROVER with the DNN.
Augmentation features do not count toward the ten, and no search in this chapter uses them (Section [REF]).
If an input cannot be parsed or embedded, it gets an all-zero row, so that every representation of a dataset keeps the same rows.
In computed descriptors, a missing or infinite value is set to 0, and values are stored unscaled.
A pretrained model gives one vector per input, the mean of its last-layer token vectors with padding excluded, unless the tables say otherwise.
Scaling and filling of missing values happen inside each fold, on the training rows only, as described in the construction of the hybrid.
The small-molecule representations (Table [REF]) are the fingerprint, descriptor, graph and language-model families described in Chapter [REF].
The only additions are four sets of 3D shape and pharmacophore features, used as augmentation only.
All four are computed from a single conformer per molecule, embedded with a fixed seed and optimized with the Merck molecular force field.
A single conformer may misdescribe flexible molecules.
Reaction datasets (Table [REF]) use three kinds of representation.
The condensed graph of reaction (CGR) merges reactants and products into one graph in which the bonds that change are marked [CIT].
Here it is hashed into a circular fingerprint after atom mapping [CIT].
Reaction language models read the reaction SMILES directly [CIT].
Any molecular representation can also be applied to the reactants, to the product, or to their difference.
A one-hot encoding of which aryl halide, ligand, base and additive was used carries no chemistry.
It is kept because on plate data such identity features can predict yield about as well as chemical descriptors [CIT].
Antibody representations (Table [REF]) start from the heavy- and light-chain amino-acid sequences.
Besides one-hot and BLOSUM62 encodings [CIT], most are frozen language models, either trained on all proteins or on antibody repertoires only.
Most models embed each chain separately and join the two vectors, so their width doubles on datasets with both chains.

Several representations read one model in different ways, for instance averaging over earlier layers or over the complementarity-determining region (CDR) residues only, with CDRs found by IMGT numbering [CIT] using ANARCI [CIT].
Datasets of point variants of one parent antibody also use features that describe each mutation.
The downstream models (Chapter [REF]) are random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, an SVM, a DNN and a Gaussian process [CIT].
Each dataset uses the two that scored best in the earlier search of the whole dataset (Table [REF]).
All six are used: the Gaussian process is one of the two models on four small antibody datasets (angiopoietin-2 binding, HIC retention, AC-SINS self-association and CHO polyreactivity).
Tree ensembles are the baseline to beat, because a hybrid is a tabular feature matrix and tree-based models still lead on medium-sized tabular data of about 10,000 samples [CIT].
By default, every model uses the same settings on every dataset, so that score differences come from the input.
An optional per-fold random search tries 20 draws of a model's settings on 3 group-aware inner folds of the outer training fold.
In the search, the DNN is not tuned this way and relies on early stopping instead.
We tested whether tuning helps on one outer fold of QM9, hERG K_i, Caco-2 efflux, LogD and Buchwald--Hartwig yield.
Each downstream model was given its two best single representations, chosen on that fold's training molecules.
The tuner tried the default and 20 draws from grids that reach stronger regularization than the optional search.
In this test the DNN was tuned as well, over dropout, learning rate and layer sizes.
The tuner scored each setting on 3 inner folds grouped by scaffold family of the training molecules, so the held-out fold never reached it.
Table [REF] gives the held-out RMSE at both settings.
The SVM gained most: on LogD with MHG-GNN, RMSE fell from 0.475 to 0.421.
Tuning made the random forest worse on Buchwald--Hartwig yield.
At default settings, two repeat fits of the DNN on QM9 with Mol2vec scored 0.487 and 0.495.
The DNN rows for Caco-2 and hERG K_i were computed before DNN predictions were capped at the range of the training labels.
With one fold, these pairs show direction only.
The Gaussian process and the SVM are skipped above the dataset sizes in Table [REF], because their fits no longer finish in useful time.
Other models left out on named datasets are listed in Additional file [REF], and all model settings are in Additional file [REF].
The kNN model is not a default downstream model.
It takes k = 5 neighbors by default, lowered to the square root of the number of training samples when a fold has fewer than 25.
It is a third downstream model in the search with the nearest-neighbor objective (Chapter [REF]), on every dataset.
Each dataset is scored in the metric its field normally uses, so that it can be compared with published work (Table [REF]).
Regression on small molecules, QM9 included, and on reaction yields uses RMSE in the label's units.
Antibody regression uses Spearman , because these assays rank candidates and their scales differ between laboratories.
Binary classification uses AUROC, which does not depend on a decision threshold.
We do not average metrics across datasets.
Each comparison is reported as its per-fold differences and their spread across the 5 folds.
We use no significance tests and no confidence intervals, because 5 fold scores are correlated through shared training molecules.
No unbiased estimator of the variance of k-fold cross-validation exists that is valid under all distributions, and estimates that ignore the overlap underestimate it [CIT].

text: We report them as computed and name the correction beside each result it affects.
Summed over its 5 outer folds, the search of one dataset took 2.3 hours (hERG K_i) to 28.2 hours (MDR1--MDCK efflux) on small molecules, and 11.1 hours on Buchwald--Hartwig yield.
On antibodies it took 0.4 hours (CHO polyreactivity) to 38.6 hours (the anti-VEGF expression scan).
The hERG K_i total is likely too low, since one of its folds recorded only 90 seconds.
Each fold ran as its own job on a CPU node of the Oxford ARC or HTC cluster, with 8 cores and 64 GB of memory by default.
The times count only each fold's last attempt, so a fold resumed from a stopped run is undercounted.
The hybrid is the best of many configurations, so its gain may only reward a large search.
Each experiment below asks one question about this or a related issue.
Table [REF] lists them, with the settings each varies and holds fixed.
Unless stated otherwise, every experiment below uses the dataset's grid (Table [REF]), its two downstream models, five outer folds and the dataset's own metric.
From each fold's search it takes, for each downstream model, the two single representations and the two hybrids with the best scores on the training samples.
As a second reference beside the best single representation, every base representation is joined, standardized on the training samples and reduced by PCA [CIT] to each budget of the dataset's grid.
The downstream model is fitted on the principal components as they are.
On each fold, the hybrid is compared with PCA at the hybrid's own budget, so neither side's width is chosen on the held-out samples.
PCA cannot have more components than training samples, so where the budget is larger the two widths differ.
The ensemble fits one model per representation and pools their predictions (late fusion), whereas the hybrid fits one model on one fused feature vector (early fusion) [CIT].
Every choice for the ensemble is made on an inner 3-fold group split of the outer training samples.
The first ensemble uses the same downstream model on every representation, and the second uses each representation's own better model.
Each picks its members, the top 3 representations or all of them.
Each also picks one of seven ways to pool predictions, from the mean and median to trimmed, outlier-removed and score-weighted means.
On each outer fold, the base representations are ranked by their summed feature importance on the training samples.
The top 1, 2 or 3 of them supply the B features with the highest importance among their own features.
These are compared with the search's own hybrid at B and with an even split of B over every base representation.
Each of these uses the importance method that the fold's best hybrid used.
The search's hybrid differs from the hand-built hybrids in two ways at once.
It ranks representations by their standalone scores rather than by summed importance, and it stops at the last feature with importance above zero.
Datasets above 2,000 samples are first reduced to about 2,000 by drawing whole scaffold families with a fixed seed.
Scaffolds at or above the 80th percentile of group size form the easy half, and the rest form the hard half.
Each half gets its own search on each outer fold.
The hybrid of a search on all the subset's training samples is also rebuilt and scored on each half.
Three other splits (by heavy-atom count, label spread within a scaffold and feature spread within a scaffold) were run and are not reported here.
The budgets are the standard list (Table [REF]) plus 4,000 and 8,000 features.
They also include 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5 and 2 times the smallest outer training set, which places one budget where the number of features equals the number of samples.
At every budget, the winning configuration is rebuilt on the outer training samples and scored on the held-out fold.
The selection bias at a budget is the search's own score minus the held-out score.
A positive value means the search promised more than the held-out fold gave.
We report how the bias changes with the budget, and the budget the search picks on each fold from its training samples alone.
We do not compare hybrids wider than the training set against narrower ones by their best held-out budgets, because that choice reads the held-out labels on both sides.
A second check repeats each outer fold's search with one more fold removed from its training samples, for each of the other four folds.
The held-out fold is the same, so the two searches differ by one fold of training samples.
Each search also picks its own budget, so the two hybrids can differ in width as well.

text: On regression datasets, every method receives B features from all base representations joined, fitted on the fold's training samples.

text: The methods are the two best hybrids at budget B from the fold's search, mRMR [CIT], recursive feature elimination [CIT] and B random features. mRMR ranks features by mutual information and stops at 200 features for run time.

subsection: Feature reduction at the same width
text: Each of the dataset's two downstream models scores every method, so only the features differ.
One search per outer fold is run for each evaluator setting.
The matched evaluator belongs to the downstream model's family.
A near-family evaluator pairs tree models with each other, the SVM with a Gaussian process, and the DNN with a narrower DNN.
A far-family evaluator pairs tree models with an SVM, the SVM with LightGBM, and the DNN with k-nearest neighbors.
A fourth setting scores the DNN with a wider DNN, and a fifth searches the dataset's own internal evaluators (Table [REF]).
Each setting's search picks its own budget, so the number of features can differ between settings.
The SVM's near-family evaluator ran before the Gaussian-process correction of 8 October 2026 on every dataset.
Importance is computed on the training samples by the method the search picked.
Sample weighting needs a model that accepts per-sample weights, so it is not run for the Gaussian process, and it is not run on multiclass tasks.
The five conditions are:
No weighting: the features as selected.
Feature weighting: standardized features multiplied by the square root of their importance, with the weights normalized to average 1.
Sample weighting: samples weighted by how well their label agrees with their 10 nearest neighbors in the rescaled space.
Combined weighting: feature and sample weighting together.
Above-median selection: only the features strictly above the median importance.
The weight of sample i is 1 - |y_i - y_N(i)| / ( y - y), clipped to lie between 0.1 and 1, where y_N(i) is the mean label of its 10 nearest neighbors by Manhattan distance.
Tree splits depend only on the order of values [CIT], so for tree models feature weighting differs from no weighting only in that zero-importance features drop out.
The rescaling does change which samples are nearest neighbors, and so changes sample weighting.
Sample weighting down-weights rather than removes a suspect label, unlike neighbor-based filtering (Section [REF]).
We found no QSAR study that does this, and learned per-sample weights for noisy labels come from general machine learning [CIT].

As a control, the embedding's selected features in the hybrid are replaced by the same number of Gaussian random features, with no new search.
